- Adults: 150 to 300 minutes a week of moderate aerobic activity, plus muscle-strengthening on at least 2 days a week. [^1] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:16
- Youth 6 to 17: at least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity daily, including muscle- and bone-strengthening. [^1] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:18
- Preschoolers 3 to 5: active through the day, about 3 hours a day of active play. [^1] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:20
- The 2nd edition removed the 10-minute minimum bout. Any length of activity counts toward the weekly total. [^1] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:22
- Its framing is "sit less, move more": some activity is better than none. [^1] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:24
- WHO 2020 (the international counterpart) for adults 18 to 64: 150 to 300 min a week moderate, or 75 to 150 min vigorous, or a mix; muscle-strengthening on 2 or more days. Strong recommendation, moderate certainty. [^2] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:27 @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:30
- Going above 300 min moderate or 150 min vigorous is a conditional recommendation, not a strong one. [^2] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:33
- Older adults 65+: the adult target plus multicomponent activity emphasising balance and strength on 3 or more days a week. Strong recommendation. [^2] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:35
- Children and adolescents 5 to 17: an average of 60 min a day moderate-to-vigorous, plus muscle- and bone-strengthening on 3 or more days. [^2] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:37
- Pregnant and postpartum women: at least 150 min a week moderate aerobic, including muscle strengthening. Strong recommendation. [^2] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:39
- Sedentary time: limit it and replace it with any activity. WHO could not quantify a sedentary threshold. [^2] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:41
- Adults with chronic conditions (hypertension, type 2 diabetes, cancer, HIV) and people with disability get the same targets, adjusted to ability. [^2] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:43
- Both documents converge, so "150 to 300 minutes a week plus two strength days" can be quoted without picking a side. WHO carries certainty ratings, which suit hedged language. [^2] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:46

## Dose-response

- 30 to 60 minutes a week of muscle-strengthening is associated with a 10 to 20% lower risk of all-cause, cardiovascular, diabetes and cancer mortality, independent of aerobic activity (16 studies). [^13] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:162
- That curve is J-shaped: no conclusive extra benefit beyond about an hour a week of muscle strengthening. [^13] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:166
- Steps and mortality (15 cohorts, 47,471 adults): risk levelled off at about 6,000 to 8,000 steps a day for adults 60+, and about 8,000 to 10,000 for adults under 60. [^14] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:168
- The highest step quartile had a 40 to 53% lower mortality risk than the lowest. [^14] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:171
- So the 10,000-step target is higher than older adults need for the mortality benefit. [^14] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:173

## Where these come from

Each source as Louise listed it in 2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/sources.md.

[^1]: [Top 10 Things to Know About the Second Edition of the Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans](https://odphp.health.gov/our-work/nutrition-physical-activity/physical-activity-guidelines/current-guidelines/top-10-things-know) — Retrieved 2026-10-07. US Office of Disease Prevention and Health Promotion (ODPHP/HHS); official summary of the Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, 2nd edition (2018), the edition currently in force.

[^2]: [Bull FC et al. World Health Organization 2020 guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour. Br J Sports Med 2020;54:1451–1462](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7719906/) — Retrieved 2026-10-07. WHO guideline development group; carries GRADE strength-of-recommendation and certainty ratings for each population.

[^13]: [Momma H et al. Muscle-strengthening activities are associated with lower risk and mortality in major non-communicable diseases: a systematic review and meta-analysis of cohort studies. Br J Sports Med. 2022](https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2021-105061) — Retrieved 2026-10-07. Peer-reviewed meta-analysis of 16 cohort studies; source of the 30–60 min/week J-shaped dose-response.

[^14]: [Paluch AE et al. Daily steps and all-cause mortality: a meta-analysis of 15 international cohorts. Lancet Public Health. 2022;7(3):e219–e228](https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lanpub/article/PIIS2468-2667(21)00302-9/fulltext) — Retrieved 2026-10-07. Pooled analysis of 15 cohorts, 47,471 adults.

cards.title: Steady, intervals and the fat-burning zone
cards.body:
# Steady, intervals and the fat-burning zone

Aerobic methods (steady-state, HIIT, polarized, tempo, fartlek), what each is good for, and the fat-burning-zone myth.

## The weekly aerobic target

- 150 to 300 min a week moderate, or 75 to 150 min vigorous, or a mix: the adult target in both the US and WHO documents. [^1] [^2] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/02-cardio-and-running.md:10
- ACSM's split: 30+ min on 5+ days moderate, or 20+ min on 3+ days vigorous. [^4] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/02-cardio-and-running.md:12
- Short bouts count. [^1] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/02-cardio-and-running.md:14

## HIIT vs steady (moderate continuous) training

- HIIT has a non-linear dose-response: about 11 min a session reached 80% of the maximal VO2max gain (about 3.45 mL/kg/min). [^20] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/02-cardio-and-running.md:56
- Moderate continuous training was linear and needed about 52 min a session for 80% of its maximal effect. Four to five times longer. [^20] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/02-cardio-and-running.md:59
- In people with cardiovascular disease, HIIT raised VO2peak more than moderate continuous training, more so in programmes longer than 12 weeks, and was safe there. [^21] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/02-cardio-and-running.md:61
- For broader cardiometabolic risk factors, HIIT and moderate continuous training were comparable. [^21] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/02-cardio-and-running.md:64
- The defensible claim is time-efficiency for fitness, not superiority across the board. [^20] [^21] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/02-cardio-and-running.md:66
- HIIT carries higher perceived exertion and higher acute musculoskeletal and cardiac risk, so gate it behind screening and a base of moderate work. [^67] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/02-cardio-and-running.md:66

## Polarized (80/20) training

- Zones in this literature: low below the first ventilatory threshold (under 2 mmol/L), moderate between thresholds (2 to 4 mmol/L), high above the second (over 4 mmol/L). [^23] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/02-cardio-and-running.md:73
- The polarized model is about 70 to 75% low, 0 to 5% moderate, 15 to 20% high, by volume. [^23] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/02-cardio-and-running.md:75
- Review of 14 studies (163 participants in all): 8 of 10 measuring VO2max improved, 5 significantly. Work economy improved significantly in 5 studies. [^23] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/02-cardio-and-running.md:76 @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/02-cardio-and-running.md:78
- Limits: small total sample, possible publication bias, short-term only. [^23] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/02-cardio-and-running.md:80
- "Mostly easy, a small slice hard" suits trained endurance athletes. For someone doing 150 min a week it is over-engineering. [^1] [^2] [^23] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/02-cardio-and-running.md:83

## Other named methods

- Tempo or threshold work sits in the moderate band between the ventilatory thresholds, the zone the polarized model minimises. [^23] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/02-cardio-and-running.md:89
- Fartlek is unstructured alternation of faster and easier running. Describe it with the talk test rather than pace. [^15] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/02-cardio-and-running.md:91
- Intervals can be prescribed through FITT: frequency, interval intensity, interval and recovery duration, and mode. [^3] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/02-cardio-and-running.md:93

## The "fat-burning zone"

- Fat oxidation rises with intensity to a peak (FatMax) at roughly 60 to 65% VO2max, then falls steeply. [^27] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/02-cardio-and-running.md:100
- Typical peak rates are 0.3 to 0.6 g/min, with large differences between people. [^27] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/02-cardio-and-running.md:102
- Fat oxidation is minimal at 85% VO2max and above, where carbohydrate dominates. [^27] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/02-cardio-and-running.md:104
- Higher-intensity work burns more total calories, so the fat proportion during a session does not decide fat loss. [^16] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/02-cardio-and-running.md:105
- The zone describes fuel mix, not fat loss. Energy balance, deficits and body-composition targets go to the nutritionist. [^16] [^27] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/02-cardio-and-running.md:109

cards.title: When to stop and point to help
cards.body:
# When to stop and point to help

The mandatory mental-health escalation: what stops coaching, and the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline.

This card is mandatory behaviour, not optional content.

## Not a mental-health provider

- The coach may teach general stress management and mind-body practice. It may not assess, diagnose or treat mental illness, and it never presents meditation, breathwork or exercise as a substitute for care. [^48] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:249

## Stop coaching and point to help when any of these appear

- Any mention of suicidal ideation, self-harm, or intent to harm others. Suicidal ideation is a documented meditation adverse event, so this applies inside meditation conversations too. [^51] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:256
- Acute crisis or acute distress of any kind. [^58] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:258
- Psychotic symptoms, dissociation, derealisation or depersonalisation during or after practice. Cognitive anomalies appeared in 25% of adverse-event studies. [^51] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:259
- Trauma history surfacing during a body scan or breath practice. Yoga and meditation for PTSD rest on low-quality evidence, which is no basis for an AI to lead trauma-focused practice. [^48] [^49] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:261
- Anxiety or depression getting worse because of practice: the two commonest adverse effects, at 33% and 27% of adverse-event studies. [^51] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:264
- Signs of disordered eating or compulsive exercise alongside exercise questions. These are clinical matters. Stop programming and refer; the food half goes to the nutritionist. [^48] [^74] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:266 @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/07-nutrition-interface-boundary-note.md:81
- Persistent unexplained fatigue with performance decline and mood change: a physician referral, never put down to training or diet alone. [^12] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/07-nutrition-interface-boundary-note.md:84

## The US resource

- The 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline: call or text 988, or chat at 988lifeline.org. 24/7 trained crisis counsellors. [^58] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:272
- More than 200 local crisis centres; a universal entry point anywhere in the US. [^58] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:274
- Spanish-language services, services for people who are Deaf or Hard of Hearing, and a connection to the Veterans Crisis Line. [^58] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:276
- It takes contacts from anyone suicidal or in emotional distress, including substance-use crisis, and from people worried about someone else. [^58] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:278
- 988 is a US service: a universal entry point anywhere in the US. [^58] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:274

The book holds no crisis resource for people outside the US. That question is on GAPS.

cards.title: Movement for mood and stress
cards.body:
# Movement for mood and stress

Exercise for depressive symptoms and stress, the evidence strength, and planning for the weeks when stress is highest.

## The evidence at a glance

- Exercise for depression: a large network meta-analysis, effects comparable to CBT, but certainty rated low to very low. [^53] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:13
- Mindfulness: as good as evidence-based therapies for anxiety and depression, but no long-term effects beyond about 2 months in one analysis. [^48] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:14
- Yoga: substantial effect on anxiety. Tai chi: high-certainty 20% fewer people who fall. Breathwork: significant pooled effects on stress, anxiety, depression. Qigong: fibromyalgia benefits with diligent practice. [^49] [^50] [^52] [^59] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:15 @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:16 @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:17 @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:18

## Exercise and depressive symptoms (BMJ 2024)

- 218 studies, 495 arms, 14,170 participants. [^53] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:28
- Effect sizes vs active controls (Hedges' g, more negative is better): walking or jogging -0.63; yoga -0.55; strength training -0.49; mixed aerobic -0.43; tai chi or qigong -0.42; aerobic plus psychotherapy -0.54; exercise plus SSRIs -0.55. [^53] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:29 @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:30 @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:31 @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:32 @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:33 @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:34 @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:35 @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:36
- In the same network: CBT alone -0.55; SSRIs alone -0.26. [^53] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:37
- Effects grew with prescribed intensity, and were stronger in groups and with clear prescriptions. [^53] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:38
- Certainty: walking or jogging low; every other mode very low. [^53] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:40
- The authors recommend exercise alongside psychotherapy and antidepressants as a core treatment. [^53] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:42
- So: exercise helps depressive symptoms, with numbers, and the certainty is low. It is never a replacement for care someone already has. [^53] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:45

## Stress

- Exercise first spikes the stress response, then people show lower cortisol and epinephrine after activity. [^55] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:51
- Norepinephrine is implicated: exercise raises it in brain regions that handle stress. [^55] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:53
- Regular exercise can lessen stress effects, improve mood, and help memory and thinking. [^55] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:56
- About five minutes of aerobic exercise can begin to stimulate anti-anxiety effects. [^55] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:58

## What people report (for coaching, not for claims)

- 53% feel good about themselves after exercising; 35% say it puts them in a good mood; 30% feel less stressed. [^54] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:64
- 43% exercise to manage stress, and 62% of those call it very or extremely effective. [^54] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:66
- But 39% of those skipped exercise in the past month when they were stressed. [^54] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:68
- Only 17% of adults exercise daily; 37% less than once a week or not at all. [^54] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:70
- Plan for adherence to drop when stress is highest. Agree a five-minute version in advance, and treat a missed week as normal, not failure. [^54] [^55] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:74

## Where these come from

Each source as Louise listed it in 2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/sources.md.

US federal research centre; the authoritative evidence-and-safety summary, including the ~8% adverse-event figure.

[^49]: [Yoga: What You Need To Know — National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NIH), page last updated August 2023](https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/yoga-what-you-need-to-know) — Retrieved 2026-10-07. US federal research centre; evidence by condition plus safety and contraindications.

[^50]: [Tai Chi: What You Need To Know — National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NIH), page last updated December 2023](https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/tai-chi-what-you-need-to-know) — Retrieved 2026-10-07. US federal research centre; source of the high-certainty 20% reduction in people who fall and the instructor-licensure note.

[^52]: [Fincham GW, Strauss C, Montero-Marin J, Cavanagh K. Effect of breathwork on stress and mental health: A meta-analysis of randomised-controlled trials. Sci Rep. 2023;13(1):432](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9828383/) — Retrieved 2026-10-07. Peer-reviewed meta-analysis of RCTs; self-report outcomes.

[^53]: [Noetel M, Sanders T, Gallardo-Gómez D, et al. Effect of exercise for depression: systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials. BMJ. 2024 Feb 14;384:e075847](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10870815/) — Retrieved 2026-10-07. 218-study network meta-analysis with CINeMA certainty ratings; doi 10.1136/bmj-2023-075847.

[^54]: [Exercise: A healthy stress reliever — American Psychological Association press release (Stress in America survey data)](https://www.apa.org/news/press/releases/stress/2013/exercise) — Retrieved 2026-10-07. APA survey data on self-reported exercise and stress management.

[^55]: [Working out boosts brain health — American Psychological Association](https://www.apa.org/topics/exercise-fitness/stress) — Retrieved 2026-10-07. APA topic page summarising research on exercise, cortisol, epinephrine and norepinephrine.

[^59]: [Mind and Body Practices for Fibromyalgia: What the Science Says — National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NIH)](https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/providers/digest/mind-and-body-practices-for-fibromyalgia-science) — Retrieved 2026-10-07. US federal research centre; source of the qigong 30–40 min/day for 6–8 weeks finding and the meditative-movement review.

cards.title: FITT-VP, the shape of a plan
cards.body:
# FITT-VP, the shape of a plan

The prescription skeleton (frequency, intensity, time, type, volume, progression) and the four training components.

## The skeleton

- ACSM's exercise prescription framework is FITT-VP: Frequency, Intensity, Time, Type, Volume, Progression. [^3] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:55
- Frequency: days a week. Intensity: how hard (%HRmax, %HRR, METs, RPE, %1RM). Time: minutes, or sets times reps. Type: aerobic, resistance, flexibility, neuromotor. Volume: MET-min a week, or weekly sets per muscle group. Progression: % load increase, added minutes or sets. [^3] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:61 @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:63 @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:64 @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:65
- FITT-VP is applied separately to each of four components: aerobic, resistance, flexibility and neuromotor. [^3] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:67
- A prescription is individualised to health status, physical ability, age, training response and the person's goals. [^3] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:69
- Intensity anchors: moderate = 3 to 5.9 METs, 64 to 76% HRmax, 45 to 63% VO2max. Vigorous = 6.0+ METs, 77 to 93% HRmax, 64 to 91% VO2max. [^3] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:71

## The weekly template (ACSM 2011 position stand)

- Aerobic: 30+ min a day on 5+ days moderate (150+ min a week), or 20+ min a day on 3+ days vigorous (75+ min a week), or a mix. [^4] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:80
- Resistance: each major muscle group on 2 to 3 days a week. [^4] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:82
- Neuromotor (balance, agility, coordination): 2 to 3 days a week. [^4] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:83
- Flexibility: stretches for each major muscle-tendon group, 60 seconds per exercise in total, on 2+ days a week. [^4] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:84
- This stand predates the 2026 resistance-training stand. Where they disagree on resistance specifics, 2026 wins. [^4] [^6] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:86

## A reasoning order for any training question

- Screen first (see the screening card). [^64] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:226
- Set the weekly target from the PAG 2nd edition or WHO numbers for that person's age and situation. [^1] [^2] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:227
- Fill the four components with FITT-VP, separately. [^3] [^4] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:67
- Choose a progression rule before choosing exercises: 2 to 10% load, two consecutive sessions; conservative single-session jumps for running. [^5] [^24] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:231
- Build recovery in by default rather than after symptoms appear. [^12] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:233
- Prefer adherence over optimisation: the largest gain is from doing none to doing some. [^8] [^9] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:234

## Where these come from

Each source as Louise listed it in 2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/sources.md.

[^1]: [Top 10 Things to Know About the Second Edition of the Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans](https://odphp.health.gov/our-work/nutrition-physical-activity/physical-activity-guidelines/current-guidelines/top-10-things-know) — Retrieved 2026-10-07. US Office of Disease Prevention and Health Promotion (ODPHP/HHS); official summary of the Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, 2nd edition (2018), the edition currently in force.

[^2]: [Bull FC et al. World Health Organization 2020 guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour. Br J Sports Med 2020;54:1451–1462](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7719906/) — Retrieved 2026-10-07. WHO guideline development group; carries GRADE strength-of-recommendation and certainty ratings for each population.

cards.title: Stretching and warming up
cards.body:
# Stretching and warming up

How much to stretch, which technique, static stretching before effort, and the RAMP warm-up.

## The flexibility prescription

- ACSM 2011: stretches for each major muscle-tendon group, 60 seconds per exercise in total, on 2+ days a week. [^4] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:11
- Static, PNF and ballistic stretching are all named as acceptable. [^4] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:13
- Neuromotor work (balance, agility, coordination, gait) is separate, on 2 to 3 days a week. [^4] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:15
- WHO folds balance into multicomponent activity on 3+ days a week for older adults. [^2] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:17

## Long-term range of motion

- Meta-analysis of 23 studies: every stretching type improved long-term range of motion. Static gave significantly greater gains than ballistic or PNF. [^36] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:22
- It suggested at least 5 minutes a week per muscle group of static stretching, and that 5+ days a week may help. [^36] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:25

## Right now: technique barely matters

- Behm et al. 2023: no significant difference between techniques for acute range of motion. [^34] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:22 @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:31
- Stretching beat no stretching with a small effect. [^34] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:35
- No relationship between hold length and gain. Holds from 5 to 900 seconds all helped. [^34] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:36
- All types can be used with similar results, regardless of intensity, duration, technique, sex, age or training status. [^34] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:39
- So prescribe total weekly time and consistency, not a hold length or technique. [^34] [^36] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:43

## Static stretching before effort: the dose is the problem

- Short static stretching (60 s or less per muscle group) inside a full warm-up trivially impairs strength and power: about 1 to 2%. [^35] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:51
- Longer (over 60 s per muscle group) gives practical declines of 4.0 to 7.5%. [^35] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:54
- One meta-analysis (104 studies): maximal strength down 5.4%, power down 1.9%. [^35] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:56
- Another (125 studies): 60 s or more per muscle group, 4.6% decline; 60 s or less, 1.1%. [^35] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:58
- Put short static stretches inside a warm-up that also has aerobic activity, dynamic stretching and sport-specific work. [^35] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:60
- Stretching showed no significant injury-prevention benefit. [^26] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:64
- The honest line: a quick static stretch before training is not harmful; holding over a minute per muscle right before a maximal effort reduces performance; stretching is not injury prevention. [^26] [^35] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:67

## The RAMP warm-up

- Four phases: Raise, Activate, Mobilise, Potentiate. [^47] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:75
- Raise: low-intensity activity lifts body temperature, heart rate, breathing and blood flow. [^47] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:76
- Activate and Mobilise: dynamic movement is favoured over static holds. [^47] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:78
- Potentiate: progressively harder, task-specific work. [^47] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:80
- In youth soccer players RAMP beat static stretching or no warm-up for sprint and jump performance. [^47] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:82
- It matches the advice that a warm-up has an aerobic part, dynamic stretching and sport-specific activity. [^35] [^47] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:60

## Where these come from

Each source as Louise listed it in 2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/sources.md.

[^2]: [Bull FC et al. World Health Organization 2020 guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour. Br J Sports Med 2020;54:1451–1462](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7719906/) — Retrieved 2026-10-07. WHO guideline development group; carries GRADE strength-of-recommendation and certainty ratings for each population.

[^4]: [Garber CE et al. American College of Sports Medicine position stand. Quantity and quality of exercise for developing and maintaining cardiorespiratory, musculoskeletal, and neuromotor fitness in apparently healthy adults: guidance for prescribing exercise. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2011 Jul;43(7):1334–59. PMID 21694556](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21694556/) — Retrieved 2026-10-07. ACSM position stand; source of the four-component weekly template including the flexibility and neuromotor numbers.

[^26]: [Lauersen JB, Bertelsen DM, Andersen LB. The effectiveness of exercise interventions to prevent sports injuries: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials. Br J Sports Med. 2014;48:871–877 (full text PDF)](https://static1.squarespace.com/static/55b7ffebe4b0568a75e3316b/t/58331e36e58c627c2abd00b5/1479745080809/Br+J+Sports+Med-2014-Lauersen-871-7.pdf) — Retrieved 2026-10-07. The reference meta-analysis on strength training, proprioception and stretching for injury prevention.

[^34]: [Behm DG, Alizadeh S, Daneshjoo A, et al. Acute Effects of Various Stretching Techniques on Range of Motion: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis. Sports Med Open. 2023;9:107](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10645614/) — Retrieved 2026-10-07. Peer-reviewed systematic review with meta-analysis and meta-regression; doi 10.1186/s40798-023-00652-x.

[^35]: [Chaabene H, Behm DG, Negra Y, Granacher U. Acute Effects of Static Stretching on Muscle Strength and Power: An Attempt to Clarify Previous Caveats. Front Physiol. 2019;10:1468](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6895680/) — Retrieved 2026-10-07. Peer-reviewed review synthesising multiple meta-analyses on the ≤60 s vs >60 s duration threshold.

[^36]: [Thomas E, Bianco A, Paoli A, Palma A. The Relation Between Stretching Typology and Stretching Duration: The Effects on Range of Motion. Int J Sports Med. 2018;39(4):243–254. PMID 29506306](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29506306/) — Retrieved 2026-10-07. Peer-reviewed meta-analysis of 23 studies; source of the 5 min/week/muscle-group minimum dose.

[^47]: [Acute effects of the RAMP warm-up on sprint and jump performance in youth soccer players. 2025](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12234454/) — Retrieved 2026-10-07. Peer-reviewed trial of Jeffreys' RAMP (Raise, Activate, Mobilise, Potentiate) warm-up framework versus static stretching and no warm-up.

cards.title: How hard should it feel
cards.body:
# How hard should it feel

Measuring intensity in practice: the talk test, heart-rate zones, RPE, METs, and the honest Zone 2 caveat.

## Everyday measures

- Talk test (CDC): at moderate intensity you can talk but not sing. At vigorous intensity you cannot say more than a few words without pausing for breath. [^15] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:182
- Moderate examples (CDC): brisk walking at 3 mph or faster, water aerobics, cycling under 10 mph on the flat, doubles tennis, ballroom dancing, general gardening. [^15] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:184
- Vigorous examples (CDC): race walking, jogging or running, swimming laps, singles tennis, aerobic dancing, cycling 10 mph or faster or with hills, jumping rope, continuous digging, hiking uphill or with a heavy pack. [^15] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:187
- Estimated maximum heart rate is 220 minus age. A 25-year-old's estimate is 195 bpm. [^16] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:190
- Zones against that estimate: light under 64% HRmax, moderate 64 to 76%, vigorous 77 to 93%. [^16] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:191
- Worked example: a 25-year-old at moderate intensity aims for roughly 125 to 148 bpm. [^16] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:193
- Consumer 5-zone watches: zones 2 to 3 usually match moderate and zone 4 vigorous. The zones can be reset to match the CDC bands. [^16] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:194
- 220 minus age is a population estimate, not a measurement. RPE and the talk test are often the more honest instruction for an untested beginner. [^3] [^15] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:196
- METs: moderate is 3 to 5.9, vigorous is 6.0 or more. [^3] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/02-cardio-and-running.md:29
- RPE on the Borg 6 to 20 scale: moderate about 12 to 13, vigorous about 14 or more. [^3] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/02-cardio-and-running.md:30

## Zone 2, and the honest caveat

- Zone 2 is usually placed at or just below the first lactate threshold, often taken as blood lactate below about 2.0 mmol/L. [^22] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/02-cardio-and-running.md:34
- Markers in use include 72 to 82% HRmax, 1.5 to 2.5 mmol/L lactate, baseline lactate plus 0.5 mmol/L, ventilatory threshold 1, 65% of peak VO2, and maximal fat-oxidation intensity. [^22] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/02-cardio-and-running.md:36
- In 50 experienced cyclists these markers did not agree. Coefficients of variation ran from 6% to 29%. [^22] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/02-cardio-and-running.md:39
- The authors conclude that percentage-based markers may not produce consistent responses across individuals. A fixed percentage can land someone too low or too high. [^22] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/02-cardio-and-running.md:42
- So present Zone 2 as easy, conversational, sustainable for an hour. Treat any HR percentage as an estimate. Never tell someone their watch's Zone 2 is physiologically right for them. [^22] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/02-cardio-and-running.md:46

## Where these come from

Each source as Louise listed it in 2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/sources.md.

[^3]: [Exercise Prescription and Basic Principles of Therapeutic Exercise — PM&R KnowledgeNow, American Academy of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation](https://now.aapmr.org/exercise-prescription-and-basic-principles-of-therapeutic-exercise/) — Retrieved 2026-10-07. Peer-reviewed professional-body reference describing ACSM's FITT-VP framework and intensity anchors.

[^15]: [How to Measure Physical Activity Intensity — Centers for Disease Control and Prevention](https://www.cdc.gov/physical-activity-basics/measuring/index.html) — Retrieved 2026-10-07. US federal public-health agency; source of the talk test and the moderate/vigorous activity examples.

[^16]: [How to train using heart-rate zones — Human Performance Resources by CHAMP (HPRC), Uniformed Services University](https://www.hprc-online.org/physical-fitness/training-performance/how-train-using-heart-rate-zones) — Retrieved 2026-10-07. US Department of Defense human-performance resource; restates CDC heart-rate bands and addresses the fat-burning-zone misconception.

[^22]: [Meixner B, Filipas L, Holmberg HC, Sperlich B. Zone 2 Intensity: A Critical Comparison of Individual Variability in Different Submaximal Exercise Intensity Boundaries. Transl Sports Med. 2025;2025:2008291](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11986187/) — Retrieved 2026-10-07. Peer-reviewed study of 50 experienced cyclists comparing eight competing Zone 2 definitions; doi 10.1155/tsm2/2008291.

cards.title: Meditation, mindfulness and breathwork
cards.body:
# Meditation, mindfulness and breathwork

What meditation and breathwork can and cannot do, their documented adverse effects, the real MBSR dose, and the disclosures that go with them.

## What the evidence says (NCCIH)

- Anxiety and depression: mindfulness approaches beat no treatment and worked as well as evidence-based therapies. [^48] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:85
- But a 2021 analysis found mixed short-term results and no long-term effects in studies beyond two months. [^48] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:87
- Chronic pain: more effective than several treatments, but the studies were low quality. Acute pain: no evidence of reduced severity. [^48] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:89 @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:91
- Blood pressure: MBSR was linked to a significant drop in people with health conditions. The AHA calls meditation a possible benefit. [^48] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:92
- Sleep: mindfulness improved sleep quality more than education and matched approaches like CBT. [^48] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:95
- PTSD: six of eight studies reported symptom reduction. Smoking and substance use: cravings fell, but relapse was not prevented better. [^48] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:97 @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:99
- Use NCCIH's hedged words: "may help", "mixed results", "evidence is not conclusive". [^48] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:101
- Never use meditation or mindfulness to replace conventional care or to put off seeing a provider. [^48] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:103

## Adverse effects: the part most fitness content leaves out

- Few studies have examined harms, so firm safety statements are not possible. [^48] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:108
- A 2020 review of 83 studies: about 8% of participants had a negative effect, similar to psychological therapies. [^48] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:110
- The most common were anxiety and depression. For MBSR, practice was not more harmful than no treatment. [^48] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:85 @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:113
- Farias et al. 2020 screened 6,742 studies; under 1% defined or measured adverse events. [^51] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:115
- Among studies that did, the most common: anxiety (33%), depression (27%), cognitive anomalies (25%), gastrointestinal problems or suicidal ideation (11% each). [^51] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:117
- Adverse events are common during or after meditation and can occur in people with no prior mental-health difficulties. [^51] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:120

## The disclosures that go with any meditation or breathwork

- Negative effects are documented at roughly 8% of participants in one review of 83 studies. Comparable to psychological therapies, not zero. [^48] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:283
- The most common are anxiety and depression, and they can occur in people with no prior history. [^51] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:285
- If practice keeps making you feel worse, stop and see a qualified teacher or clinician. [^48] [^51] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:287
- Meditation and breathwork are never a reason to delay seeing a provider. [^48] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:289

## The real MBSR dose

- Standard MBSR: 8 weeks of weekly 2.5-hour classes (up to 3.5), plus an all-day silent retreat of about 7.5 hours in week 6. [^56] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:131
- Home practice up to 45 minutes daily with guided audio. [^57] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:134
- A 2.5-hour orientation and a 5 to 10 minute interview come first. [^56] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:135
- Core practices: awareness of breath, body scan, walking meditation, mindful movement, open awareness. [^57] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:137
- The trial evidence rests on 20+ hours of class and 45 min a day of practice. App micro-sessions do not inherit MBSR's effect sizes. [^48] [^56] [^57] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:140

## Breathwork (meta-analysis of RCTs, 2023)

- Anxiety (20 studies): g -0.32. Depressive symptoms (18 studies): g -0.40. [^52] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:153 @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:154
- Conclusion: breathwork may improve stress and mental health. Outcomes were self-reported. [^52] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:152 @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:155
- Slow paced breathing with a longer exhale is a reasonable, low-risk tool, with a small-to-moderate effect stated honestly. [^52] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:158
- High-intensity or hyperventilation protocols are outside what this coach leads without supervision. [^51] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:158

## Where these come from

Each source as Louise listed it in 2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/sources.md.

[^48]: [Meditation and Mindfulness: Effectiveness and Safety — National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NIH), page last updated June 2022](https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/meditation-and-mindfulness-effectiveness-and-safety) — Retrieved 2026-10-07. US federal research centre; the authoritative evidence-and-safety summary, including the ~8% adverse-event figure.

[^51]: [Farias M, Maraldi E, Wallenkampf KC, Lucchetti G. Adverse events in meditation practices and meditation-based therapies: a systematic review. Acta Psychiatr Scand. 2020;142(5):374–393](https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/Adverse-events-in-meditation-practices-and-a-review-Farias-Maraldi/eaacd57a3ad72cc85e8d71afbddb74d52a5b06f5) — Retrieved 2026-10-07. Peer-reviewed systematic review; the primary source on meditation adverse-event types and frequencies.

[^52]: [Fincham GW, Strauss C, Montero-Marin J, Cavanagh K. Effect of breathwork on stress and mental health: A meta-analysis of randomised-controlled trials. Sci Rep. 2023;13(1):432](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9828383/) — Retrieved 2026-10-07. Peer-reviewed meta-analysis of RCTs; self-report outcomes.

[^56]: [Santorelli SF (ed.). Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR): Standards of Practice, 2014 (University of Massachusetts Center for Mindfulness, PDF)](https://mindfulness.au.dk/fileadmin/mindfulness.au.dk/Artikler/Santorelli_mbsr_standards_of_practice_2014.pdf) — Retrieved 2026-10-07. The originating centre's formal standards document for MBSR programme structure.

[^57]: [Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction Teacher Training Participant Packet, 2024 — UC San Diego Center for Integrative Health (PDF)](https://cih.ucsd.edu/sites/cih.ucsd.edu/files/mbpti/MBSR-TTI-Participant-Booklet_2024.pdf) — Retrieved 2026-10-07. University MBSR teacher-training materials; source of the daily home-practice dose and core practice list.

cards.title: The line with the nutritionist
cards.body:
# The line with the nutritionist

What the coach answers and what it hands to the nutritionist, the anabolic-window myth, and handoff wording.

## The line

- The nutritionist owns intake: dietary frameworks, therapeutic diets, allergies, life-stage nutrition, meal prep, food safety, and the fuelling side of exercise (pre- and post-workout food, protein timing and totals, hydration volumes, electrolytes, carbohydrate periodisation, supplements). [^75] [^76] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/07-nutrition-interface-boundary-note.md:11 @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/07-nutrition-interface-boundary-note.md:13 @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/07-nutrition-interface-boundary-note.md:14 @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/07-nutrition-interface-boundary-note.md:15
- The coach owns what the body does: training, intensity, volume, progression, technique, recovery practice, sleep, mobility, mind-body practice, screening, red flags and scope refusals. [^4] [^12] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/07-nutrition-interface-boundary-note.md:20 @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/07-nutrition-interface-boundary-note.md:21 @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/07-nutrition-interface-boundary-note.md:22

## The four recurring seams

- "What should I eat before or after lifting?" The coach answers session structure and when to train; the food goes to the nutritionist. [^4] [^75] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/07-nutrition-interface-boundary-note.md:29
- "How do I lose fat?" The coach answers the training programme and intensity; energy balance, intake and deficit size go to the nutritionist. [^16] [^27] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/07-nutrition-interface-boundary-note.md:30
- "Should I take creatine or protein powder?" The coach answers nothing and refers in full. [^76] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/07-nutrition-interface-boundary-note.md:31
- "I'm always exhausted after sessions." The coach answers load, progression, sleep, deloads and the overtraining referral; energy availability and intake go to the nutritionist. [^12] [^75] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/07-nutrition-interface-boundary-note.md:32

## The anabolic-window myth

- Protein within 1 hour after lifting had a small hypertrophy effect vs waiting 2+ hours, but it all but disappeared once total protein intake was controlled. [^75] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/07-nutrition-interface-boundary-note.md:40
- There is a lack of evidence for a narrow anabolic window. [^75] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/07-nutrition-interface-boundary-note.md:44
- With adequate total daily protein, timing has a limited independent effect. [^75] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/07-nutrition-interface-boundary-note.md:46
- NSCA practitioner material treats the anabolic window as needing this same correction. [^76] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/07-nutrition-interface-boundary-note.md:48
- Say: total daily protein matters much more than the half-hour after a session. How much protein, and how to spread it, is a nutrition question. Then route. [^75] [^76] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/07-nutrition-interface-boundary-note.md:51

## Training facts that look like food but are not

- The fat-burning zone describes fuel mix, not fat loss; the coach corrects the zone claim and routes deficits. [^16] [^27] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/07-nutrition-interface-boundary-note.md:61
- Avoiding cold water right after lifting, when growth is the goal, is a recovery-timing decision. [^39] [^40] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/07-nutrition-interface-boundary-note.md:65
- Supplements for soreness (such as tart cherry) appear in recovery papers, but any supplement is the nutritionist's. [^37] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/07-nutrition-interface-boundary-note.md:69
- Sleep extension of 46 to 113 minutes is recovery, not diet. [^42] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/07-nutrition-interface-boundary-note.md:72

## Shared escalation

- Disordered eating or compulsive exercise: stop programming and refer; the crisis-line card and 988 apply. [^58] [^74] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/07-nutrition-interface-boundary-note.md:81
- Persistent unexplained fatigue, performance decline and mood change: a physician referral from either agent. Never put it down to training or diet alone. [^12] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/07-nutrition-interface-boundary-note.md:84

## Wording the coach can reuse

- "That's a nutrition question, and I'd rather not guess at it. It belongs with the nutritionist. What I can tell you is the training side." @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/07-nutrition-interface-boundary-note.md:93
- "The timing part matters less than people think. The totals part isn't mine to answer." [^75] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/07-nutrition-interface-boundary-note.md:97

cards.title: Overload, progression and periodization
cards.body:
# Overload, progression and periodization

How a plan advances, what specificity and detraining mean, and how much periodization matters.

## Progression

- Overload: adaptation needs a stimulus greater than the body is used to, so the programme must advance. [^3] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:93
- Progression must be gradual. Advancing too quickly is the main avoidable risk in exercise prescription. [^3] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:95
- The concrete rule (ACSM 2009): increase load by 2 to 10% once the person can do 1 to 2 reps beyond the target on two consecutive sessions. [^5] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:97
- Specificity: adaptations are specific to the mode, muscles, velocity and energy systems trained. That is why the four components are prescribed separately. [^3] [^4] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:100
- Detraining: maximal force does not drop measurably in under 7 days off. The drop becomes significant only after about the third week. [^46] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:103

## Periodization: real, but smaller than the industry implies

- Meta-analysis (81 effects, 18 studies, 1988 to 2015): periodized resistance training gave greater 1RM gains than non-periodized, effect size 0.43. [^10] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:111
- That analysis found publication bias. Removing the outsized studies roughly halved the effect, though it stayed significant. [^10] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:113
- Gains were greater in untrained people, and with higher frequency and longer duration. The advantage is partly a proxy for training more and longer. [^10] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:115
- Linear periodization: high volume and low intensity moving to low volume and high intensity over months. [^11] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:118
- Undulating periodization: loading varies daily, weekly or every two weeks. [^11] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:120
- Linear vs undulating for strength: one meta-analysis found no difference; later ones suggested undulating gave greater maximal strength. [^11] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:121
- Linear vs undulating for hypertrophy: two meta-analyses found no advantage to either. [^11] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:123
- Whether periodized beats non-periodized for hypertrophy specifically is unclear. Most studies are short and rarely include tapers. [^11] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:124 @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:126
- For general-population clients, periodization is an optional organising device, not a requirement. A beginner does not need a mesocycle chart. [^8] [^9] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:129

cards.title: Soreness, recovery and rest
cards.body:
# Soreness, recovery and rest

What DOMS is, which recovery methods help when, cold water and muscle growth, sleep, deloads, tapers, detraining, and overtraining.

## DOMS: what it is, and what it is not

- DOMS is local muscle tenderness, stiffness and pain arising 24 to 72 h after eccentric or high-intensity exercise. [^37] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:96
- It is self-limiting, peaks within 1 to 7 days, and usually resolves within a week. [^37] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:98
- DOMS does not come from lactic acid. That theory is now considered obsolete. [^37] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:100
- Current mechanisms: microtrauma and sarcomere disruption from eccentric loading, connective-tissue damage, an inflammatory cascade, nociceptor sensitisation (especially in fascia), and satellite cells in repair. [^37] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:102
- Peak soreness falls at 24 to 72 h. [^38] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:106
- Soreness is not a measure of workout quality. It comes from unaccustomed eccentric loading. [^37] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:109

## Recovery methods: what helps, and when (22 RCTs)

- Jump performance at 24 h: active recovery ranked best, then cold-water immersion. [^38] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:124
- Soreness right after: massage strongest; cold water also helped. At 24 h massage still ranked first. [^38] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:125 @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:126
- Soreness at 48 h: only cold-water immersion kept a significant benefit. [^38] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:127
- Creatine kinase (muscle-damage marker): only cold water reduced it acutely. [^38] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:128
- Overall, recovery effects depend on timing: active recovery for short-term power, massage for early soreness, cold water for broader short-term support. [^38] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:130
- Active recovery and light activity repeatedly ease DOMS, which favours light movement over complete rest. [^37] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:133
- Foam rolling: benefits look mainly mechanical (tone, flexibility); pain relief is inconsistent. [^37] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:136
- Compression garments are endorsed for treatment and prevention of DOMS. [^37] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:138
- Static stretching for DOMS offers no meaningful clinical benefit. [^37] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:140
- Contrast baths add nothing over cold water alone. [^37] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:143
- Cryosauna at -110 °C, 48 to 72 h after exercise, reduced stiffness, leukocytes and creatine kinase. [^37] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:144

## Cold water and muscle growth

- Meta-analysis of 8 RCTs: resistance training alone gave more hypertrophy than training plus cold-water immersion. Small effect, 95.7% probability it favoured training alone. [^39] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:151 @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:155
- If muscle growth is the priority, avoid cold water immediately after lifting. The finding applies to immediate post-exercise cooling. [^39] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:160
- Study quality was fair to poor, so the conclusion is directional, not settled. [^39] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:162
- Mechanism: cold water reduces mTORC1 signalling, shifting protein balance toward breakdown. [^40] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:164
- Over 12 weeks of twice-weekly training it has been reported to blunt hypertrophy and isometric strength gains. [^40] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:166
- Two uses of cold: acute soreness relief (supported) vs a routine habit after lifting when growth is the goal (a small cost). Not immediately after resistance sessions, and not by default. [^38] [^39] [^40] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:173

## Sleep

- Most elite athletes get less than the recommended 7 to 9 hours. [^41] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:183
- National Sleep Foundation: 7 to 9 hours for adults 18 to 64. [^41] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:185
- Sleep extension of 46 to 113 minutes is the proposed range for athletes who sleep about 7 hours. [^42] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:186
- Extension improved sprint times, shooting accuracy, tennis serve accuracy and endurance. [^41] [^42] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:188
- Naps of 20 to 90 minutes can improve performance and restore it after partial sleep loss. [^42] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:190
- Sleep is a primary recovery variable. [^43] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:192
- "Aim to add 45 to 60 minutes" is more useful than "sleep more". [^41] [^42] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:195
- Persistent unrefreshing sleep, loud snoring with witnessed pauses, or daytime sleepiness that extension does not fix: a medical referral, not coaching. [^12] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:195

## Rest days, deloads, tapers, breaks

- Deloads are commonly planned every 4 to 8 weeks. [^77] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:205
- Typical coach-prescribed deload week: 1 to 2 sessions, 30 to 60 min, 1 to 3 sets, 1 to 6 reps, 60 to 84% 1RM. [^45] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:206
- A 1-week deload in the middle of a 9-week programme hurt lower-body strength and did not help hypertrophy, power or endurance. [^44] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:208
- A taper before competition is different and helps: 2 to 8% better strength performance. [^77] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:213
- Under 7 days off is unlikely to cost strength. The drop becomes significant only after about the third week. [^46] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:215
- Tell apart a taper (supported), a routine mid-cycle deload (not supported for strength) and a short break (costs almost nothing). [^44] [^46] [^77] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:221
- Rest days remain because the guideline is 2 to 3 resistance days a week, not daily. [^4] [^7] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:221

## Overreaching and overtraining

- Functional overreaching: a short dip that turns into improvement after recovery. Normal training. [^12] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:141
- Non-functional overreaching: training and recovery out of balance; the dip persists. [^12] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:233
- Overtraining syndrome is told apart only by clinical outcome and exclusion. There is no confirmatory test. [^12] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:146
- No marker (hormonal, performance, psychological, biochemical, immune) meets accepted criteria. [^12] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:148
- Never label someone as overtrained. Describe the pattern (lasting performance drop, mood change, poor sleep despite less load) and refer to a physician: the differential includes anaemia, thyroid disease, depression and infection. [^12] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/01-exercise-science-foundations.md:151 @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:238
- In-scope responses: cut volume rather than frequency, protect sleep, keep activity light rather than stopping, and escalate if performance and mood do not recover. [^12] [^37] [^41] [^42] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/04-mobility-flexibility-recovery.md:241

Peer-reviewed systematic review (Sleep Medicine Reviews); source of the 46–113 min extension range and the 20–90 min nap guidance.

PeerJ. 2024;12:e16777](https://peerj.com/articles/16777/) — Retrieved 2026-10-07. Peer-reviewed controlled trial; the mid-programme deload showed worse lower-body strength outcomes.

PMID 39446750](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39446750/) — Retrieved 2026-10-07. Peer-reviewed survey documenting what coaches actually prescribe in a deload week.

Peer-reviewed practical review; source of the 4–8 week deload interval convention and the 2–8% taper improvement figure.

cards.title: Refuse and refer, or proceed with care
cards.body:
# Refuse and refer, or proceed with care

The checklist for when the coach declines to build a plan and refers, and when it proceeds with caution.

## Decline to build a plan, and refer, when

- Screening finds known cardiovascular, metabolic or renal disease, or symptoms of it, in someone not currently exercising. [^64] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/06-special-populations-and-safety.md:344
- Any absolute contraindication is present. [^68] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/06-special-populations-and-safety.md:346
- Resting blood pressure is over 200/110 mmHg, or hypertension is uncontrolled. [^31] [^68] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/06-special-populations-and-safety.md:347
- The person is pregnant and has, or may have, an absolute contraindication, or has not discussed exercise with their obstetric provider. [^62] [^63] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/06-special-populations-and-safety.md:348
- The person reports chest pain, fainting or near-fainting, unexplained severe breathlessness, palpitations, or a fever. [^64] [^68] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/06-special-populations-and-safety.md:350
- A suspected concussion or any acute head injury. [^71] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/06-special-populations-and-safety.md:352
- An undiagnosed or acute muscle, bone or joint injury: physical-therapist scope. [^74] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/06-special-populations-and-safety.md:353
- A minor wants strength programming without qualified in-person supervision. [^32] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/06-special-populations-and-safety.md:354
- A cancer survivor in a situation where the consensus advises medical clearance. [^70] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/06-special-populations-and-safety.md:356
- Any mental-health red flag: see the crisis-line card, and point to 988. [^51] [^58] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/06-special-populations-and-safety.md:358

## Proceed, with explicit caution and modification, when

- The person is 65+: add balance work and start load low. [^2] [^31] [^60] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/06-special-populations-and-safety.md:363
- The person has controlled hypertension, type 2 diabetes or arthritis, or is a cleared cancer survivor. [^31] [^61] [^69] [^70] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/06-special-populations-and-safety.md:364
- The person was inactive and wants vigorous training: build a moderate base first, because sudden unaccustomed vigorous effort is where the transient cardiac risk concentrates. [^67] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/06-special-populations-and-safety.md:366

## Where these come from

Each source as Louise listed it in 2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/sources.md.

cards.title: Running load, injury and a first 5k
cards.body:
# Running load, injury and a first 5k

How fast to build running, what actually prevents running injuries, and a couch-to-5k style template built from the evidence.

## The real signal is the single session, not the week

- Best current evidence: the Garmin-RUNSAFE Running Health Study (BJSM 2025). [^24] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/02-cardio-and-running.md:119
- 5,205 runners (mean age 45.8, 22% female); 1,820 (35%) had a running-related injury across 588,071 sessions. [^24] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/02-cardio-and-running.md:122
- Overuse injury rose when a single session exceeded 110% of the longest run in the previous 30 days. [^24] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/02-cardio-and-running.md:124
- Hazard rate ratios vs staying at or under +10%: small spike (over 10 to 30%) 1.64; moderate (over 30 to 100%) 1.52; large (over 100%) 2.28. [^24] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/02-cardio-and-running.md:126
- The week-to-week ratio showed no relationship with injury. The acute:chronic workload ratio showed a negative dose-response. [^24] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/02-cardio-and-running.md:128
- Earlier: a 13-week programme at about +10% a week showed no difference in injuries from an 8-week programme at about +24% a week. [^25] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/02-cardio-and-running.md:130
- So replace "no more than 10% more mileage a week" with "keep any single run within about 10% of your longest run in the last month." [^24] [^25] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/02-cardio-and-running.md:134
- For questions about whether someone's own habits are a risk factor, the companion RUNSAFE analysis of self-reported training characteristics is the source. [^29] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/02-cardio-and-running.md:140 @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/02-cardio-and-running.md:142

## What prevents injuries

- Lauersen et al. (BJSM 2014), a meta-analysis of RCTs on injury prevention. [^26] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/02-cardio-and-running.md:147
- Strength training cut sports injuries to less than a third of control levels, and overuse injuries by almost half. [^26] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/02-cardio-and-running.md:149
- Proprioceptive training cut injury risk by roughly 45%. [^26] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/02-cardio-and-running.md:151
- Stretching showed no significant injury-prevention benefit. [^26] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/02-cardio-and-running.md:152
- For a runner asking how to stay healthy, the first answer is two strength sessions a week and conservative single-session jumps, not stretching. [^24] [^26] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/02-cardio-and-running.md:156
- Training parameters are consistently implicated in running injuries, though that evidence base was limited. [^25] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/02-cardio-and-running.md:161
- Biomechanical risk factors call for injury-specific analysis, so no single gait or cadence cue can be offered as general injury prevention. [^28] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/02-cardio-and-running.md:163 @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/02-cardio-and-running.md:165

## A first-5k template (a template, not a prescription for one person)

- Weeks 1 to 3, frequency first: 3 sessions a week of walk/run intervals, 20 to 30 min a session, run segments at talk-test moderate. [^1] [^15] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/02-cardio-and-running.md:175
- Progression rule: lengthen run segments so no single session exceeds about 110% of the longest continuous run in the last 30 days. [^24] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/02-cardio-and-running.md:178
- Strength from week 1: two sessions a week for hips, glutes, quadriceps and calves. [^26] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/02-cardio-and-running.md:180
- Weeks 4 to 8, consolidate: keep 3 runs a week. One can grow toward 30 continuous minutes while the others stay short. Weekly moderate minutes should pass 150 around here. [^1] [^2] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/02-cardio-and-running.md:182
- Weeks 9 to 12: add one faster session (intervals or tempo). About 11 min of interval work a session captures 80% of the achievable VO2max effect. [^20] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/02-cardio-and-running.md:185
- Do not add static stretching as a warm-up fix. It does not reduce injury, and long holds impair the next effort. [^26] [^35] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/02-cardio-and-running.md:188
- Step-back weeks reduce volume rather than stopping. Strength is not meaningfully lost in under 7 days. [^46] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/02-cardio-and-running.md:190
- Say plainly that this is a template, and screen first. [^64] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/02-cardio-and-running.md:172

## Cardio for health outcomes (training side)

- Aerobic training improves glycaemic management in type 2 diabetes (ACSM 2022). [^69] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/02-cardio-and-running.md:199
- Isometric exercise gave the largest resting blood-pressure drop of any mode (270 RCTs): about 8.24 mmHg systolic, 4.00 diastolic. The wall squat ranked highest. [^33] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/02-cardio-and-running.md:201
- Walking or jogging had the largest antidepressant effect of any mode in a 218-study network meta-analysis (Hedges' g -0.63). [^53] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/02-cardio-and-running.md:204

## Where these come from

Each source as Louise listed it in 2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/sources.md.

[^1]: [Top 10 Things to Know About the Second Edition of the Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans](https://odphp.health.gov/our-work/nutrition-physical-activity/physical-activity-guidelines/current-guidelines/top-10-things-know) — Retrieved 2026-10-07. US Office of Disease Prevention and Health Promotion (ODPHP/HHS); official summary of the Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, 2nd edition (2018), the edition currently in force.

[^2]: [Bull FC et al. World Health Organization 2020 guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour. Br J Sports Med 2020;54:1451–1462](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7719906/) — Retrieved 2026-10-07. WHO guideline development group; carries GRADE strength-of-recommendation and certainty ratings for each population.

[^15]: [How to Measure Physical Activity Intensity — Centers for Disease Control and Prevention](https://www.cdc.gov/physical-activity-basics/measuring/index.html) — Retrieved 2026-10-07. US federal public-health agency; source of the talk test and the moderate/vigorous activity examples.

[^20]: [Optimising Exercise Prescription: A Meta-Analysis Examining the Dose Response of Exercise Duration on Cardiorespiratory Fitness Following HIIT and MICT. Sports Med. 2026](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02528-y) — Retrieved 2026-10-07. Peer-reviewed dose-response meta-analysis; source of the ~11 min vs ~52 min per session figures.

[^24]: [How much running is too much? Identifying high-risk running sessions in a 5200-person cohort study. Br J Sports Med. 2025;59(17):1203–1210 (full text PDF)](https://findresearcher.sdu.dk/ws/files/295073070/1203.full.pdf) — Retrieved 2026-10-07. Garmin-RUNSAFE Running Health Study; doi 10.1136/bjsports-2024-109380. The strongest current evidence on running training load and overuse injury.

[^25]: [Nielsen RO et al. Training errors and running related injuries: a systematic review. Int J Sports Phys Ther. 2012;7(1):58–75](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3290924/) — Retrieved 2026-10-07. Peer-reviewed systematic review; includes the 10%/week vs 24%/week comparison.

[^26]: [Lauersen JB, Bertelsen DM, Andersen LB. The effectiveness of exercise interventions to prevent sports injuries: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials. Br J Sports Med. 2014;48:871–877 (full text PDF)](https://static1.squarespace.com/static/55b7ffebe4b0568a75e3316b/t/58331e36e58c627c2abd00b5/1479745080809/Br+J+Sports+Med-2014-Lauersen-871-7.pdf) — Retrieved 2026-10-07. The reference meta-analysis on strength training, proprioception and stretching for injury prevention.

[^28]: [Running-Related Biomechanical Risk Factors for Overuse Injuries in Distance Runners: A Systematic Review Considering Injury Specificity and the Potentials for Future Research. 2022](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9325808/) — Retrieved 2026-10-07. Peer-reviewed systematic review arguing for injury-specific rather than pooled biomechanical analyses.

[^29]: [Using Self-Reported Training Characteristics to Better Understand Who Is More Likely to Sustain Running-Related Injuries Than Others: The Garmin-RUNSAFE Running Health Study. 2024](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11664494/) — Retrieved 2026-10-07. Companion analysis from the same prospective cohort as [^24].

Br J Sports Med. 2023;57:1317–1326](https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care/20230817/running-wall-sits-most-effective-exercises-for-high-blood-pressure) — Retrieved 2026-10-07. Medical trade publication summary of a 270-RCT network meta-analysis.

Front Physiol. 2019;10:1468](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6895680/) — Retrieved 2026-10-07. Peer-reviewed review synthesising multiple meta-analyses on the ≤60 s vs >60 s duration threshold.

Peer-reviewed study on detraining time course; basis for the "<7 days costs little" statement.

[^53]: [Noetel M, Sanders T, Gallardo-Gómez D, et al. Effect of exercise for depression: systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials. BMJ. 2024 Feb 14;384:e075847](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10870815/) — Retrieved 2026-10-07. 218-study network meta-analysis with CINeMA certainty ratings; doi 10.1136/bmj-2023-075847.

[^64]: [Whitfield GP et al. Applying the ACSM Preparticipation Screening Algorithm to U.S. Adults: National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey 2001-2004. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2017. PMID 28557860](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28557860/) — Retrieved 2026-10-07. [^69]: [Exercise/Physical Activity in Individuals with Type 2 Diabetes: A Consensus Statement from the American College of Sports Medicine.
