University-hosted detailed breakdown of the Fragala et al. 2019 statement, including the frailty progressions and safety guidance.

[^60]: [Older Adult Activity: An Overview — Centers for Disease Control and Prevention](https://www.cdc.gov/physical-activity-basics/guidelines/older-adults.html) — Retrieved 2026-10-07. US federal public-health agency; the 65+ aerobic, strengthening and balance targets and the muscle-group list.

cards.title: Yoga, tai chi and qigong
cards.body:
# Yoga, tai chi and qigong

What yoga, tai chi and qigong are good for, how strong that evidence is, and how to do them safely.

## Yoga (NCCIH, 2023)

- Low-back pain: slightly better than no exercise; differences may be clinically small. [^49] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:169
- Neck pain: less pain and disability. Headaches: fewer and milder, especially tension headaches. [^49] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:171 @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:172
- Knee osteoarthritis: may improve pain, function and stiffness. [^49] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:174
- Anxiety: a substantial beneficial effect. Depression: helps when combined with other treatments. PTSD: only low-quality evidence of possible benefit. [^49] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:175 @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:176 @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:177
- Sleep improvements in cancer patients, people with arthritis and older adults. Balance improved in 11 of 15 studies. [^49] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:178 @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:180
- Menopause: at least as effective as other exercise. Smoking: 37% more likely to quit during treatment. [^49] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:181 @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:182
- In the depression network meta-analysis yoga's effect was g -0.55, second to walking or jogging. [^53] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:183

## Yoga safety

- Generally safe for healthy people with a qualified instructor. [^49] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:188
- Commonest injuries: sprains and strains, mostly knee or lower leg. Serious injuries are rare. [^49] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:190
- Emergency-department injury rates are higher in people 65+. [^49] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:192
- Pregnancy: avoid hot yoga and long periods lying on the back. If lying back makes you light-headed or unwell, change position. [^49] [^62] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:198
- Beginners avoid extreme poses such as headstands and lotus. [^49] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:195
- Modify for prior injuries, spinal disease, hypertension, balance problems and glaucoma. [^49] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:196

## Tai chi (NCCIH, 2023)

- Falls in older adults: low-certainty evidence of 19% fewer falls, and high-certainty evidence of 20% fewer people who fall. [^50] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:207
- Parkinson's: fewer falls vs no intervention. Stroke: better walking short-term. [^50] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:210 @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:212
- Osteoarthritis: the American College of Rheumatology strongly recommends tai chi for knee and hip OA; evidence low-to-moderate. [^50] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:213
- Fibromyalgia, low-back pain, blood pressure, COPD and cognition: benefits reported. [^50] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:216 @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:218 @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:220 @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:222 @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:223
- Depression and anxiety: a small effect in older adults with chronic conditions. [^50] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:225
- Safety: adverse events were similar to other active or no intervention, and minor. [^50] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:227
- Instructors need no licence, and there is no national certification standard. [^50] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:230
- Tai chi is the best-supported recommendation for balance and fall prevention in older adults, and it fits WHO's balance advice and ACSM's neuromotor component. [^2] [^4] [^50] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:238

## Qigong and meditative movement

- Qigong in fibromyalgia: 30 to 40 minutes daily for 6 to 8 weeks gave consistent benefits in pain, sleep and function, still present 4 to 6 months later. [^59] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:232
- Tai chi, qigong and yoga gave modest improvements in sleep, fatigue, mood and quality of life, continuing at 3 to 6 months. [^59] @2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/05-mind-body-mental-wellness.md:234

## Where these come from

Each source as Louise listed it in 2026-10-07-health-and-fitness-agent/sources.md.

[^2]: [Bull FC et al. World Health Organization 2020 guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour. Br J Sports Med 2020;54:1451–1462](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7719906/) — Retrieved 2026-10-07. WHO guideline development group; carries GRADE strength-of-recommendation and certainty ratings for each population.

[^4]: [Garber CE et al. American College of Sports Medicine position stand. Quantity and quality of exercise for developing and maintaining cardiorespiratory, musculoskeletal, and neuromotor fitness in apparently healthy adults: guidance for prescribing exercise. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2011 Jul;43(7):1334–59. PMID 21694556](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21694556/) — Retrieved 2026-10-07. ACSM position stand; source of the four-component weekly template including the flexibility and neuromotor numbers.

[^49]: [Yoga: What You Need To Know — National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NIH), page last updated August 2023](https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/yoga-what-you-need-to-know) — Retrieved 2026-10-07. US federal research centre; evidence by condition plus safety and contraindications.

[^50]: [Tai Chi: What You Need To Know — National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NIH), page last updated December 2023](https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/tai-chi-what-you-need-to-know) — Retrieved 2026-10-07. US federal research centre; source of the high-certainty 20% reduction in people who fall and the instructor-licensure note.

[^53]: [Noetel M, Sanders T, Gallardo-Gómez D, et al. Effect of exercise for depression: systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials. BMJ. 2024 Feb 14;384:e075847](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10870815/) — Retrieved 2026-10-07. 218-study network meta-analysis with CINeMA certainty ratings; doi 10.1136/bmj-2023-075847.

[^59]: [Mind and Body Practices for Fibromyalgia: What the Science Says — National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NIH)](https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/providers/digest/mind-and-body-practices-for-fibromyalgia-science) — Retrieved 2026-10-07. US federal research centre; source of the qigong 30–40 min/day for 6–8 weeks finding and the meditative-movement review.

[^62]: [Pregnancy — Canadian Society for Exercise Physiology guidelines (2019 Canadian Guideline for Physical Activity throughout Pregnancy; Mottola MF et al., Br J Sports Med 2018;52:1339–1346)](https://csepguidelines.ca/guidelines/pregnancy/) — Retrieved 2026-10-07. National professional-body guideline; the clearest publicly accessible list of absolute and relative contraindications to exercise in pregnancy.

cards.title: Celiac disease and gluten, and three thresholds kept apart
cards.body:
# Celiac disease and gluten

## The thresholds, kept apart
- FDA's rule of 2 August 2013: a food may say "gluten-free" if it has under 20 ppm gluten. [^28] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:94
- 20 ppm was chosen because methods could not reliably detect gluten below it. [^28] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:95
- About 10 mg of gluten a day is safe for the vast majority of people with celiac disease. [^29] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:96
- Celiac disease affects about 1 in 100 people worldwide. [^29] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:98
- Keep the legal threshold (20 ppm), the body's threshold (about 10 mg a day) and kitchen evidence apart. Mixing them causes fear or false safety. [^28] [^29] [^32] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:115

## Where gluten hides
- Gluten comes from wheat, barley and rye, and turns up in many non-obvious products, so label reading is the core skill. [^30] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:102
- Oats are easily contaminated: buy oats labelled gluten-free. [^30] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:103
- "Wheat-free" is not "gluten-free": it does not cover barley or rye. [^30] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:152

## The kitchen
- Cross-contact is when a gluten-free food meets a gluten-containing ingredient, making it unsafe. [^31] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:104
- Separate equipment is the conventional advice, including a dedicated toaster. [^31] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:105
- A preliminary study found no significant gluten transfer from a shared toaster (stayed under 20 ppm). [^32] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:109
- A pilot study of shared fryers is the source for restaurant fryer questions. [^33] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:110
- Separate equipment stays the default; measured studies can refine it, not replace it. [^31] [^32] [^33] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:153

## Where the agent stops
- May teach label reading and kitchen separation. [^34] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:119
- Diagnosis needs blood tests and a biopsy before gluten comes out. Never advise starting gluten-free before testing; route to a gastroenterologist. [^34] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:119
- NIDDK's guidance covers the practical diet and recommends a dietitian. [^34] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:111

cards.title: My cookbook: where its recipes come from
cards.body:
# My cookbook: where its recipes come from

- My cookbook holds 102 recipes: 24 breakfasts, 25 lunches, 30 dinners, 6 sides, 3 snacks and 14 treats. [^12] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/07-cookbook.md:5
- 74 come from the VA's Nutrition and Food Services recipe library, and each names its own page there. [^14] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/07-cookbook.md:6
- 28 come from the NHLBI's heart-healthy recipes, and each names its own page there. [^15] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/07-cookbook.md:7
- By their ingredients, 72 are vegetarian, 25 vegan, 58 gluten-free (with labels checked), 49 dairy-free and 86 nut-free. [^12] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/07-cookbook.md:8
- "Low sodium" on a label means 140 mg of sodium or less per serving. [^13] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/07-cookbook.md:9
- "No salt added" means none was added in processing; the food may still have sodium. [^13] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/07-cookbook.md:10
- The Daily Value for sodium is less than 2,300 mg a day. [^13] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/07-cookbook.md:11

cards.title: Diabetes and prediabetes, what the ADA says and where the agent stops
cards.body:
# Diabetes and prediabetes

- The ADA routes personal medical nutrition therapy to an RDN, preferably one experienced in diabetes (Recommendation 5.10). [^23] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:13
- The ADA endorses no single meal plan and no set macronutrient percentages. It individualises to goals, body and medicines. [^23] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:14
- Emphasise non-starchy vegetables, whole fruit, legumes, lean protein, whole grains, nuts, seeds, and low-fat or non-dairy alternatives. [^23] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:15
- Minimise red meat, sugary drinks, sweets, refined grains, and processed and ultra-processed food. [^23] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:16
- The 2026 Standards suggest considering less carbohydrate for some adults with diabetes, with limiting processed food as an effective route. [^23] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:17
- Fiber: at least 14 g per 1,000 kcal. [^5] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:18
- Protein: about 0.8 g/kg/day. [^5] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:19
- Saturated fat under 10% of calories, about 22 g on 2,000 kcal. [^5] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:20
- Sodium under 2,300 mg a day. [^5] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:21
- The ADA favours Mediterranean-style and DASH-like patterns. [^5] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:22
- Red meat is linked to higher type 2 diabetes risk in a dose-dependent way, which favours plant protein. [^5] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:23
- The ADA publishes a Summary of Revisions every year: re-check it each January. [^24] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:24
- The conflict: the DGA's 1.2-1.6 g/kg/day protein sits well above the ADA's 0.8, and may harm people with undiagnosed kidney disease. [^5] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:30
- The DGA also allows full-fat dairy (3 servings a day) and butter while keeping the under-10% saturated-fat cap, a practical conflict in diabetes. [^5] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:32

## Where the agent stops
- May explain carb counting, glycaemic ideas, fiber targets, label reading and the general shape of Mediterranean and DASH eating. [^5] [^13] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:36
- Must refuse insulin-to-carb ratios, matching carbs to medicine, or a carb gram target for a specific person. That is an RDN's job. [^23] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:37
- Never suggest during-exercise carb or electrolyte protocols to a person with diabetes without their clinician. [^23] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/05-nutrition-exercise-interface.md:191

cards.title: Eating patterns with the best outcome evidence (AHA, DASH), caffeine and alcohol
cards.body:
# Eating patterns, caffeine and alcohol

## The AHA heart-healthy pattern
- The AHA's 2021 scientific statement supersedes its 2006 diet and lifestyle statement. [^12] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:216
- Its ten features: keep a healthy weight; plenty of varied fruit and vegetables; whole grains; mostly plant protein, fish, low-fat dairy, lean unprocessed meat if wanted; liquid plant oils over tropical oils; minimally processed over ultra-processed food; little added sugar; little or no salt; don't start drinking alcohol and limit it if you do; apply it wherever food is made or eaten. [^12] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:223

## DASH
- Daily servings at 2,000 kcal: grains 6-8, vegetables 4-5, fruit 4-5, meat/poultry/fish 6 or fewer, low-fat dairy 2-3, fats and oils 2-3. [^13] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:228
- Weekly: 4-5 servings of nuts, seeds, beans and peas; 5 or fewer of sweets. Sodium capped at 2,300 mg a day; 1,500 mg lowers blood pressure further. [^13] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:231
- The DASH-Sodium trial fed 412 adults with untreated raised blood pressure through three 30-day sodium levels. [^14] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:235
- DASH plus low sodium gave systolic pressure 11.5 mm Hg lower than control diet plus high sodium in people with hypertension. [^14] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:236
- On DASH the sodium steps gave smaller drops (1.3 and 1.7 mm Hg) than on the control diet: the two help, but overlap rather than fully stack. [^14] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:238

## Heart disease and blood pressure
- The AHA pattern is the backbone, with DASH plus sodium reduction as the measured intervention. [^12] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:74
- Teach the pattern and the sodium arithmetic. Never manage someone on diuretics, potassium-sparing drugs or warfarin without their clinician. [^47] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:86

## Caffeine
- The FDA cites 400 mg a day as not generally linked to harm in healthy adults. [^17] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:242
- The FDA estimates toxic effects such as seizures from rapid intake of about 1,200 mg. [^17] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:243
- Pure and highly concentrated caffeine products have caused deaths. [^17] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:244
- No caffeinated drinks under age 2; medical experts advise against energy drinks for children and teens. [^17] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:245

## Alcohol
- AHA: if you don't drink, don't start; if you do, limit it. [^12] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:246

cards.title: Food allergies, lactose intolerance, and swapping safely
cards.body:
# Food allergies and intolerances

## The nine major US allergens and the label law
- The nine: milk, eggs, fish, crustacean shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat, soybeans, sesame. [^41] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:182
- Sesame became the ninth under the FASTER Act and must be labelled from 1 January 2023. [^41] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:183
- Makers must declare it in one of three places: the ingredient list by common name, a "Contains" statement, or in brackets after the ingredient. [^41] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:184
- "May contain" statements are not covered by the mandatory rule. [^41] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:185

## How common
- Convincing food allergy in US adults: about 10.8%. [^42] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:189
- In children: about 8.0%. [^43] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:190
- Most common in adults: shellfish 2.9%, milk 1.9%, peanut 1.8%, tree nut 1.2%. [^42] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:191

## Preventing peanut allergy: early, not avoidance
- NIAID published its peanut-prevention addendum in January 2017, after the LEAP trial. [^44] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:196
- LEAP enrolled 640 infants aged 4-11 months with severe eczema, egg allergy, or both. [^45] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:197
- Infants who ate peanut through age 5 had an 81% lower risk of peanut allergy. [^45] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:198
- Introduce peanut foods to all infants before age 1, from about 4-6 months, once they can manage solids. [^45] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:199
- Infants with moderate-to-severe eczema or egg allergy are highest risk and are tested first; others need no test. [^45] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:200
- The agent explains the guideline. It must refuse to direct an at-home introduction for a high-risk infant, and route to an allergist. [^45] [^44] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:204

## Lactose intolerance: an intolerance, not an allergy
- Many people with lactose intolerance can have 12 g lactose, about 1 cup of milk, without real symptoms. [^46] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:208
- Small portions with meals, gradual reintroduction, and yogurt or hard cheeses (cheddar, Swiss), which are lower in lactose. [^46] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:209
- Lactase enzyme products widen tolerance. [^46] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:210
- Hidden lactose: bread, baked goods, processed foods, cereals, processed meats, coffee creamers. Label words: milk, whey, curds, dry milk solids. [^46] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:211
- Non-dairy calcium: fish with soft bones, leafy greens, broccoli, oranges, almonds, fortified products. [^46] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:212
- Default to finding the dose, not elimination, and contrast it with milk allergy, where strict avoidance applies. [^46] [^41] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:216

## Swapping safely: the procedure at the stove
- First decide: allergy (strict avoidance plus cross-contact control) or intolerance (dose management). [^41] [^46] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:148
- For each of the nine allergens, check all three declaration places. [^41] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:149
- Re-check on every purchase. "May contain" is outside the mandatory rule and no substitute for it. [^41] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:150
- Gluten: use products labelled gluten-free (legally under 20 ppm); buy oats labelled gluten-free. [^28] [^30] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:151
- Control cross-contact with separate equipment by default. [^31] [^32] [^33] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:153
- Lactose: swap toward lower-lactose dairy or lactase, not full elimination. [^46] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:154
- When dairy comes out, replace the calcium. [^46] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:155
- Scan for hidden lactose words in bread, cereals, processed meats and creamers. [^46] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:156

cards.title: Food safety, cooking temperatures, the danger zone and storage
cards.body:
# Food safety

These are the one set of numbers the agent states flatly, with no "consult a professional" wrapper. Hedging on 165°F for poultry is worse than useless. [^68] [^67] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:53

## Safe minimum internal temperatures
- Poultry, all types: 165°F. [^68] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:15
- Ground beef, pork, veal, lamb: 160°F. [^68] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:16
- Whole cuts of beef, pork, veal, lamb: 145°F, then a 3-minute rest. [^68] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:17
- Fish and shellfish: 145°F, or until the flesh is opaque. [^67] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:18
- Reheated leftovers: 165°F. [^68] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:19
- During the rest the temperature holds or rises, which finishes off the pathogens. [^68] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:22
- Only a food thermometer tells you. Colour and texture are not reliable. [^68] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:23

## The danger zone and the two-hour rule
- The danger zone is 40°F-140°F, where bacteria multiply fast. [^69] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:27
- Never leave perishable food out more than 2 hours, or 1 hour above 90°F. [^67] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:28
- Fridge at 40°F or below; freezer at 0°F or below. [^67] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:29
- Thaw in the fridge, in cold water or in the microwave, never on the counter. [^67] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:31
- Wash hands at least 20 seconds with soap. [^67] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:32

## Storage
- Cooked meat or poultry leftovers keep 3 to 4 days in the fridge at 40°F. [^71] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:36
- Chicken nuggets or patties and pizza also keep 3 to 4 days. [^71] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:37
- For anything else, point to FoodSafety.gov's Cold Food Storage Chart rather than guess a shelf life. [^71] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:39
- FSIS has separate pages for freezing and for refrigeration, for quality-versus-safety questions. [^79] [^80] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:40

## The four steps
- Clean, Separate, Cook, Chill. [^67] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:44
- Clean: hands 20 seconds, and surfaces. [^67] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:46
- Separate: raw food apart from ready-to-eat food. [^67] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:47
- Cook: to the temperatures above. [^67] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:48
- Chill: refrigerate promptly, inside the 2-hour window. [^67] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:49

cards.title: Which guidance anchors the numbers (DRIs, the 2025-2030 DGA, WHO)
cards.body:
# Which guidance anchors the numbers

Every fact below has its page, its line and its footnote in the book. The footnote's full source is in the book's `sources.md`.

## The two US frameworks
- The Dietary Reference Intakes (DRIs) come from the National Academies and are revised nutrient by nutrient, not on a fixed cycle. [^6] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:13
- The Dietary Guidelines for Americans (DGA) are the federal food-pattern policy, revised every 5 years by USDA and HHS. [^1] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:14
- The current edition is the 10th, Dietary Guidelines for Americans 2025-2030, published January 2026, headline "Eat Real Food". [^1] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:15
- The full 2025-2030 text and scientific report live at RealFood.gov. [^2] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:16
- Name the edition and date whenever a DGA number is quoted. Any cached figure has a shelf life. [^1] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:21

## The 2025-2030 DGA is contested, so say so
- It promotes 1.2-1.6 g protein per kg per day, 50-100% above the 0.8 g/kg/day RDA. [^2] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:29
- It left the protein AMDR (10-35% of calories for adults) unchanged. [^6] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:30
- It keeps limits of under 10% of calories from saturated fat, under 10% from added sugars, and under 2,300 mg sodium a day. [^5] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:31
- Stanford's nutrition group holds that the protein target plus red meat, full-fat dairy, butter and beef tallow makes the saturated-fat ceiling hard or impossible to hit. [^3] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:32
- A published critical analysis calls this "a dietary paradox". [^4] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:33
- Stanford flagged factual errors: olive oil, butter and beef tallow listed as "healthy fats", and xylitol miscategorised. [^3] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:34
- Stanford notes fiber, which Americans under-eat, is under-emphasised. [^3] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:35
- Stanford raises an equity objection to the dairy emphasis, since about 75% of the world is lactose intolerant. [^3] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:36
- The DGA protein target conflicts with the ADA's about 0.8 g/kg/day for diabetes, and fewer than 15% of people with CKD know they have it. [^5] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:37
- When quoting a contested DGA figure, say so in one clause and name the disagreement. Do not arbitrate between USDA and the specialty societies. [^5] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:41

## WHO cross-check numbers
- Fruit and vegetables, adults 10+: at least 400 g a day. [^11] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:47
- Fruit and vegetables, children 6-9: at least 350 g a day; children 2-5: at least 250 g a day. [^11] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:48
- Naturally occurring fiber, adults: at least 25 g a day. [^11] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:49
- Free sugars: under 10% of energy, under 5% for added benefit. [^11] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:50
- Total fat at most 30% of energy. [^11] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:51
- Saturated fat at most 10% of energy. [^11] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:52
- Trans fat at most 1% of energy. [^11] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:53
- Salt under 5 g a day (about 2 g sodium). [^11] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:54
- Potassium at least 90 mmol a day (3,510 mg). [^11] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:55
- WHO sets protein at 10-15% of energy and carbohydrate at about 45-75%. [^11] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:57

cards.title: IBS and low-FODMAP, GERD and PCOS, where guidelines rate popular advice weak
cards.body:
# IBS, GERD and PCOS

## IBS and the low-FODMAP diet
- The ACG's 2021 IBS guideline recommends a limited trial of low-FODMAP for global symptoms. [^35] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:127
- That is a conditional recommendation on very low quality evidence. [^35] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:128
- Its complexity and deficiency risk need a properly trained GI dietitian. [^35] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:129
- Even so, it is the most evidence-based dietary approach for IBS. [^35] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:130
- Phase 1, low FODMAP: restrict high-FODMAP foods under a dietitian, for 2-6 weeks. [^36] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:137
- Phase 2, reintroduction: retest FODMAP groups one by one, about 6-8 weeks. [^36] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:138
- Phase 3, personalisation: long term, restricting only the groups the person reacts to. [^36] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:139
- Phase 1 is not a diet for life. The restriction exists to learn, then is relaxed. [^36] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:142
- The agent may explain the phases and say plainly that phase 1 should not run indefinitely. It must not design or supervise one. [^35] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:147
- Never write permanent low-FODMAP recipes. [^36] [^35] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:162

## GERD (reflux)
- Weight loss in overweight people helps symptoms: moderate evidence, strong recommendation. [^38] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:153
- No meals within 2-3 hours of bed: low evidence, conditional recommendation. [^38] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:154
- Avoiding individual "trigger foods": low evidence, conditional recommendation. [^38] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:155
- So never recite "avoid coffee, chocolate, tomatoes" as fact. Say the evidence is low and conditional. [^38] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:160

## PCOS
- The 2023 international guideline finds no evidence that any one diet composition beats another, for any outcome. [^39] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:166
- Lifestyle change (exercise, or diet plus exercise plus behaviour) is recommended for everyone with PCOS. [^39] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:168
- Healthy eating and activity are recommended for all women with PCOS. [^40] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:169
- A healthy lifestyle helps even without weight loss. [^40] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:170
- This is where internet claims (keto, "insulin-resistance diets", inositol protocols) get parroted. The guideline's finding: sticking with it matters more than the composition. [^39] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:174

cards.title: Kidney disease and dialysis, explain the ranges and never set them
cards.body:
# Chronic kidney disease (CKD) and dialysis

This is the hardest refusal in the knowledge. The agent explains; a renal dietitian prescribes.

- The reference is the KDOQI 2020 nutrition-in-CKD guideline. [^26] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:43
- CKD 3-5, stable, not on dialysis: 0.55-0.60 g/kg/day (a low-protein diet). [^25] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:47
- CKD 3-5, very-low-protein route: 0.28-0.43 g/kg/day plus keto-acid or amino-acid analogues. [^25] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:48
- CKD 3-5 with diabetes: 0.6-0.8 g/kg/day per KDOQI; KDIGO states 0.8 g/kg/day. [^27] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:49
- CKD 5D on haemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis, stable: 1.0-1.2 g/kg/day. [^25] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:50
- KDIGO recommends under 2 g sodium a day for diabetes and CKD. [^27] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:54
- KDOQI's guideline uses 2.3 g a day, and the groups judged the gap not clinically meaningful. [^27] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:55
- KDOQI favours vegetable protein sources, on observational evidence rather than trials. [^27] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:56

## How strong the evidence is
- A 2009 Cochrane review found protein restriction "may slow progression to kidney failure, but to a nonsignificant degree". [^27] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:60
- Later meta-analyses showed more benefit in type 1 than type 2 diabetes. [^27] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:61

## Where the agent stops
- Must refuse to set a protein, potassium, phosphorus or sodium prescription for anyone with CKD or on dialysis. It is managed like a medicine and needs a renal dietitian. [^25] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:66
- May explain the guideline ranges and why they differ on dialysis, and recommend a renal RDN. [^25] [^26] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:67
- Must flag high-protein advice as unsafe when kidney function is unknown, because most CKD is undiagnosed. [^5] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:68
- Do not adapt recipes for a renal diet: those prescriptions are clinician-set. [^25] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:163
- Sports protein ranges do not apply to anyone with CKD. [^25] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/05-nutrition-exercise-interface.md:172

cards.title: Reading a label, estimating energy needs, and why processing matters
cards.body:
# Labels, energy needs, processing

## Reading a Nutrition Facts label
- 5% DV or less per serving is low; 20% DV or more is high. [^10] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:170
- Nutrients to get less of: saturated fat, sodium, added sugars. [^10] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:171
- Nutrients to get more of: dietary fiber, vitamin D, calcium, iron, potassium. [^10] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:172
- Serving size describes typical eating. It is not a recommendation. [^10] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:173

## Estimating energy needs (Mifflin-St Jeor)
- The Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics: measure resting metabolic rate (RMR) by indirect calorimetry if possible; if not, use Mifflin-St Jeor with actual body weight. A Strong (Conditional) recommendation. [^9] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:183
- Men: RMR = (9.99 × weight kg) + (6.25 × height cm) − (4.92 × age) + 5. [^9] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:185
- Women: RMR = (9.99 × weight kg) + (6.25 × height cm) − (4.92 × age) − 161. [^9] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:186
- In people with obesity it lands within 10% of measured RMR in about 70%, overestimating up to 9% and underestimating up to 21%. [^9] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:190
- It is less accurate in obese than non-obese adults (about 75% against 87% in one analysis). [^9] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:191
- It was not validated in racial groups other than White participants. [^9] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:192
- Give a range with the error band (up to 9% over, 21% under). Never a single calorie number: the false precision is the harm. [^9] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:196

## Processing changes how much people eat
- In a 4-week inpatient crossover trial (n=20), diets matched for presented calories, sugar, fat, sodium, fiber and macros still diverged: intake was 508 ± 106 kcal a day higher on the ultra-processed diet. [^15] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:200
- People gained 0.9 kg on the ultra-processed diet and lost 0.9 kg on the unprocessed one. [^15] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:201
- The extra came from carbohydrate and fat, not protein. [^15] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:202
- NIH calls it the first RCT directly comparing intake and weight on ultra-processed against unprocessed diets. [^16] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:204
- Asked "calories or food quality?": answer with this trial. Processing changed spontaneous intake by about 500 kcal a day at matched macros. [^15] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:208
- The 2025-2030 DGA is vague on what counts as a problem processed food, so describe processing concretely: packaged, ready-to-eat, multi-ingredient, industrially formulated. [^3] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:186

cards.title: Who is asking, then infants, children, older adults and sex differences
cards.body:
# Life stages

## Fill these before any number
- Several values move 2x or more across life stages: iron 8 to 27 mg, folate 400 to 600 µg, protein 46 to 71 g. So "who is asking" comes first. [^6] [^7] [^8] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:13
- Age band (infant, child, adolescent, adult, 51+, 71+). [^6] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:17
- Sex, and pregnancy or breastfeeding. [^6] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:18
- Activity load, which changes energy and sometimes protein and fluid. [^81] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:19
- Known medical conditions and medicines. [^23] [^47] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:20

## Infants (0-12 months)
- The AAP recommends exclusive breastfeeding for about 6 months. [^55] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:26
- All breastfed infants should get at least 400 IU vitamin D a day from the first few days. [^56] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:27
- No honey in any form in the first year: infant botulism. [^54] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:29
- No cow's milk as a drink before 12 months. [^54] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:30
- No added salt or sugar in homemade baby food; avoid canned foods high in both. [^54] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:31
- Peanut foods from about 4-6 months; test first only infants with moderate-to-severe eczema or egg allergy. [^45] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:34
- From age 1, 2 servings a week of lower-mercury fish, 1 oz servings at ages 1-3. [^52] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:35
- No caffeinated drinks under 2. [^17] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:36
- Relay the published rules only. Faltering growth, reflux, suspected milk-protein allergy or prematurity go to the paediatrician. [^55] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:40

## Children and teens
- Fat AMDR is wider in young children: 30-40% of energy at 1-3 years. [^6] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:46
- Fiber AI climbs: 19 g (1-3), 25 g (4-8), 26-31 g (9-13), 38 g boys 14-18, 26 g girls 14-18. [^6] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:49
- Protein RDA: 13 g (1-3), 19 g (4-8), 34 g (9-13), 52 g boys 14-18, 46 g girls 14-18. [^6] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:50
- WHO fiber for children: 15 g (2-5) and 21 g (6-9). [^11] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:52
- Fish serving sizes scale with age: 1 oz (1-3), 2 oz (4-7), 3 oz (8-10), 4 oz (11). [^52] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:53
- Energy drinks are advised against for children and teens. [^17] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:54
- The 2025-2030 DGA advises avoiding added sugars entirely, especially for children. [^2] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:55
- Iron needs split at menarche, and boys' and girls' protein and fiber values separate at 14. [^6] [^8] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:58

## Older adults (51+, 71+)
- Calcium rises to 1,200 mg (women 51+, men 71+), and its UL drops to 2,000 mg at 51+. [^8] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:109
- Vitamin D rises to 800 IU above 70. [^7] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:110
- Women's iron falls from 18 to 8 mg after menopause. [^8] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:112
- Fiber AI falls with energy needs: 30 g men 51+, 21 g women 51+. [^6] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:113
See the protein card for protein in older adults.

## Men and women, ages 19-50
- Iron: men 8 mg, women 18 mg before menopause. [^8] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:137
- Zinc: men 11 mg, women 8 mg. [^8] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:138
- Magnesium: men 400-420 mg, women 310-320 mg. [^90] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:146
- Potassium: men 3,400 mg, women 2,600 mg. [^8] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:147
- Fiber: men 38 g, women 25 g. [^6] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:148
- Total water: men 3.7 L, women 2.7 L. [^6] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:149
- Mifflin-St Jeor differs by sex only in its constant: +5 for men, −161 for women. [^9] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:152

cards.title: Macronutrients and water by life stage
cards.body:
# Macronutrients and water

## AMDR: share of total energy
- Ages 1-3: carbohydrate 45-65%, protein 5-20%, fat 30-40%. [^6] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:69
- Ages 4-18: carbohydrate 45-65%, protein 10-30%, fat 25-35%. [^6] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:70
- Ages 19+: carbohydrate 45-65%, protein 10-35%, fat 20-35%. [^6] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:71

## RDA or AI per day (carb g, protein g, fiber g, total water)
- Ages 1-3: carb 130, protein 13, fiber 19, water 1.3 L. [^6] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:81
- Ages 4-8: carb 130, protein 19, fiber 25, water 1.7 L. [^6] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:82
- Ages 9-13: carb 130, protein 34, fiber 26-31, water 2.1-2.4 L. [^6] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:83
- Males 14-18: carb 130, protein 52, fiber 38, water 3.3 L. [^6] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:84
- Males 19+: carb 130, protein 56, fiber 30-38, water 3.7 L. [^6] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:85
- Females 14-18: carb 130, protein 46, fiber 26, water 2.3 L. [^6] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:86
- Females 19-50: carb 130, protein 46, fiber 25, water 2.7 L. [^6] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:87
- Females 51+: carb 130, protein 46, fiber 21, water 2.7 L. [^6] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:88
- Pregnancy: carb 175, protein 71, fiber 28, water 3.0 L. [^6] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:89
- Lactation: carb 210, protein 71, fiber 29, water 3.8 L. [^6] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:90
- Total water counts all beverages plus the water in food. [^6] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:75

## Notes that travel with these numbers
- The adult protein RDA is 0.8 g/kg/day; 56 g and 46 g are reference-body-weight conversions of it. [^6] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:94
- There is no RDA or AI for total fat in anyone over 12 months, only the AMDR. [^6] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:95
- The 130 g/day carbohydrate RDA supplies the brain's glucose need. It is not a cap. [^6] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:96
- An alternative fiber target in wide clinical use is at least 14 g per 1,000 kcal, which the ADA applies. [^5] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:97
- Label Daily Values: fiber 28 g, added sugars 50 g, saturated fat 20 g, sodium 2,300 mg. [^10] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:98

cards.title: Planning the week, shopping on a budget, and the weekly workflow
cards.body:
# Meal planning and budget shopping

## Plan first, then shop
- Plan before shopping, to save time and money. [^72] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:60
- Nutrition.gov offers a sample 7-day Mediterranean meal plan, as an example, not a prescription. [^72] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:64
- It offers a weekly meal planner with a grocery list, a weekly menu planner, and a seasonal produce guide. [^72] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:67
- "Shop with Meals in Mind" uses tracking lists to cut food waste. [^72] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:69
- A meal prep guide for college students is the closest federal guide to batch cooking. [^72] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:71

## The SNAP-Ed order for a tight budget
- 1. Plan to use the food already at home first. [^73] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:76
- 2. Know how much money there is for food. [^73] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:77
- 3. Make the list from that budget and what the planned meals need. [^73] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:78
- 4. Buy only what can be used before it spoils. [^73] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:79
- SNAP-Ed calls this skill set Food Resource Management. [^74] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:82
- The shopping list is made from the meal plan, never separately. That is also what prevents waste. [^73] [^72] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:86

## Reference budgets
- USDA publishes four food plans at rising cost: Thrifty, Low-Cost, Moderate-Cost and Liberal. [^76] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:94
- Each is re-priced every month with the Consumer Price Index (CPI-U). [^76] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:95
- The monthly reports give costs by age and sex, weekly and monthly. [^76] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:96
- Never hard-code a grocery budget figure: it goes stale within weeks. This agent has no current figure and says so. [^76] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:101

## What healthy food costs (no figures kept here; the book has them)
- USDA ERS priced 155 fruits and vegetables in cup equivalents at 2022 national average prices. [^77] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:105
- Meeting the fruit and vegetable recommendations was possible at a low daily cost in 2022 prices. [^77] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:106
- Of 93 vegetables, 19 fell in the cheapest price band, including baked white potato, iceberg lettuce and onions. [^78] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:109
- The cheapest items per cup equivalent were fresh watermelon and dried pinto beans. [^78] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:110

## Shopping tactics
- Use unit pricing to compare products, alongside the Nutrition Facts label. [^75] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:118
- Use all forms of produce: fresh, frozen and canned. [^73] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:120
- Buy what is in season or on sale. [^73] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:121
- Frozen and canned fruit is available all year, can save money, and has similar nutrition to fresh. [^73] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:122
- Watch sodium (and sugar) in canned food. [^54] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:124

## The weekly workflow
- 1. Inventory first: plan to eat what is already at home. [^73] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:194
- 2. Set the budget, against the current USDA food plan for the household. [^73] [^76] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:195
- 3. Choose the pattern: DASH- or Mediterranean-shaped unless a condition says otherwise. [^13] [^5] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:196
- 4. Build the menu, then derive the grocery list from it. [^72] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:197
- 5. Price the produce: in season, on sale, frozen or canned where cheaper. [^73] [^77] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:198
- 6. Lean on legumes: dried pinto beans were the cheapest cup equivalent in the ERS data. [^78] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:199
- 7. Shop with unit prices and the label's 5%/20% DV rule. [^75] [^10] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:200
- 8. Batch cook, then chill fast: out of the danger zone within 2 hours (1 hour above 90°F). [^69] [^67] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:201
- 9. Cook to temperature with a thermometer. [^68] [^67] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:202
- 10. Label and date leftovers: 3-4 days in the fridge; reheat to 165°F. [^71] [^68] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:203
- 11. Freeze the overflow at 0°F or below before day five. [^67] [^70] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:204
- 12. Close the loop: tracking lists to cut waste next time. [^72] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:205

cards.title: A batch-prep day for the week
cards.body:
# A batch-prep day for the week

- Start whatever cooks longest first, and run the oven, the stovetop and the slow cooker at the same time. [^9] [^10] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/04-batch-prep.md:5
- The evening before: clear two fridge shelves, set out clean containers, and move frozen meat to the fridge to thaw. [^10] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/04-batch-prep.md:6
- One 2 to 2.5 hour session can cover the week: a sheet-pan protein in the oven, a pot of grains and a pot of chili or soup on the stove, then egg cups once the oven is free. [^9] [^10] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/04-batch-prep.md:7
- While those cook, chop the week's vegetables and portion out frozen vegetables. [^10] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/04-batch-prep.md:8
- Spread cooked rice on a sheet pan so it cools quickly, or portion it straight into containers. [^10] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/04-batch-prep.md:9
- Portion into single meals before chilling; shallow containers cool fastest. [^10] [^3] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/04-batch-prep.md:10
- Eat the fridge meals first, through day 4, and freeze the portions for days 5 to 7. [^9] [^10] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/04-batch-prep.md:11
- Move the next frozen portions to the fridge the evening before; they thaw in 24 to 36 hours. [^10] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/04-batch-prep.md:12
- Label frozen portions with what is inside and the date. [^10] [^6] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/04-batch-prep.md:13
- Freeze burrito bowls without the salsa, and add it fresh when you eat. [^10] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/04-batch-prep.md:14
- Rotate sauces and toppings so one batch tastes different across the week. [^9] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/04-batch-prep.md:15
- Where a report gives a longer fridge time than the federal chart, the chart wins: soups, stews and egg casseroles keep 3 to 4 days. [^1] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/04-batch-prep.md:16
- Vegetarian swap for a batch chili: tofu crumbles and an extra can of beans in place of the ground meat. [^9] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/04-batch-prep.md:17
- Dairy-free swap: unsweetened soy milk for milk, and crumbled firm tofu for cottage cheese. [^9] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/04-batch-prep.md:18
- Gluten-free swap: rice, potatoes, corn tortillas and tamari in place of wheat bread, pasta and soy sauce. [^9] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/04-batch-prep.md:19

cards.title: Cooling, reheating and thawing a batch safely
cards.body:
# Cooling, reheating and thawing a batch safely

- Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour when it is above 90°F. [^3] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/02-cool-reheat-thaw.md:5
- Throw away perishable food left at room temperature longer than that. [^3] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/02-cool-reheat-thaw.md:6
- Bacteria grow fast between 40°F and 140°F; keep hot food at 140°F or warmer. [^3] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/02-cool-reheat-thaw.md:7
- Cool a batch fast by splitting it into shallow containers: a big pot of soup cools too slowly. [^3] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/02-cool-reheat-thaw.md:8
- Cut large items such as roasts into smaller pieces before chilling them. [^3] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/02-cool-reheat-thaw.md:9
- Hot food can go straight into the fridge, or into an ice or cold-water bath first. [^3] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/02-cool-reheat-thaw.md:10
- Cover, wrap airtight or seal leftovers in containers, then refrigerate or freeze them right away. [^3] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/02-cool-reheat-thaw.md:11
- Reheat leftovers to 165°F on a food thermometer. [^3] [^5] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/02-cool-reheat-thaw.md:12
- Bring sauces, soups and gravies to a rolling boil when reheating them. [^3] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/02-cool-reheat-thaw.md:13
- In the microwave, cover and vent the dish, stir or rotate it, and check the temperature in several places: microwaves leave cold spots. [^3] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/02-cool-reheat-thaw.md:14
- Frozen leftovers can be reheated without thawing: soups and stews in a pan or microwave, casseroles in the oven or microwave. [^3] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/02-cool-reheat-thaw.md:15
- Cooking or reheating from frozen takes about one and a half times as long. [^4] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/02-cool-reheat-thaw.md:16
- Thaw food in the fridge, in cold water or in the microwave; never on the counter. [^4] [^5] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/02-cool-reheat-thaw.md:17
- Fridge thawing is slowest but safe the whole time: small items thaw overnight, most foods take a day or two. [^4] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/02-cool-reheat-thaw.md:18
- Cold-water thawing: seal the food in a leak-proof bag, change the water every 30 minutes, and cook it right after. [^4] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/02-cool-reheat-thaw.md:19
- Cook food thawed in the microwave right away. [^4] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/02-cool-reheat-thaw.md:20
- Leftovers thawed in the fridge keep 3 to 4 more days, or can be refrozen. [^3] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/02-cool-reheat-thaw.md:21
- Food thawed in cold water or the microwave is cooked before it is refrozen. [^3] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/02-cool-reheat-thaw.md:22
- Freeze leftovers within 3 to 4 days. [^4] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/02-cool-reheat-thaw.md:23
- Never refreeze food that sat out of the fridge longer than 2 hours (1 hour above 90°F). [^4] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/02-cool-reheat-thaw.md:24
- Wash hands at least 20 seconds with soap, and use one board for raw meat and another for produce. [^5] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/02-cool-reheat-thaw.md:25

cards.title: What freezes well, what does not, and how to pack it
cards.body:
# What freezes well, what does not, and how to pack it

- Almost any food can be frozen; canned food and eggs in the shell are the exceptions. [^4] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/03-freezing.md:5
- Some foods freeze safely but come back poorly, such as mayonnaise, cream sauce and lettuce. [^4] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/03-freezing.md:6
- Cooked egg white turns tough, soft or spongy in the freezer. [^6] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/03-freezing.md:7
- Cooked pasta loses its texture when frozen. [^6] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/03-freezing.md:8
- Mature potatoes turn grainy, watery or dark when frozen. [^6] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/03-freezing.md:9
- Fried foods turn soggy and taste stale after freezing. [^6] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/03-freezing.md:10
- Mayonnaise, sour cream and cream sauces separate in the freezer. [^6] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/03-freezing.md:11
- Raw apples and grapes turn mushy when frozen. [^6] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/03-freezing.md:12
- Salad vegetables (cabbage, celery, cucumbers, lettuce, tomatoes) go limp and water-logged. [^6] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/03-freezing.md:13
- Cheese and crumb toppings go soggy: add them when you reheat. [^6] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/03-freezing.md:14
- Pepper, cloves and garlic can turn strong in the freezer, so season lightly and adjust when serving. [^6] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/03-freezing.md:15
- Raw meat and poultry keep their quality frozen longer than cooked, because cooking takes out moisture. [^4] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/03-freezing.md:16
- For best quality: casseroles 2 to 3 months, soups and stews 2 to 3 months, cooked meat 2 to 3 months, cooked poultry 4 months, frozen dinners 3 to 4 months. [^4] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/03-freezing.md:17
- Combination main dishes are best used within three months. [^6] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/03-freezing.md:18
- Pack food in the serving sizes you will use. [^6] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/03-freezing.md:19
- Label each package with what it is and the date. [^6] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/03-freezing.md:20
- Freeze fast: lay new packages in one layer and stack them only once they are frozen solid. [^4] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/03-freezing.md:21
- A food 2 inches thick should freeze through in about 2 hours. [^4] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/03-freezing.md:22
- Freezer burn (grayish-brown dry spots) hurts quality, not safety: cut it away. [^4] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/03-freezing.md:23
- Freezing does not destroy nutrients. [^4] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/03-freezing.md:24

cards.title: How long food keeps in the fridge and freezer
cards.body:
# How long food keeps in the fridge and freezer

- Keep the fridge at 40°F or below and the freezer at 0°F or below. [^5] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/01-cold-storage.md:5
- Freezer times are for quality only: food kept at 0°F stays safe indefinitely. [^1] [^4] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/01-cold-storage.md:6
- Product dates are not a guide to safe use; go by the storage chart. [^2] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/01-cold-storage.md:7
- Soups and stews, vegetable or meat added: 3 to 4 days in the fridge, 2 to 3 months in the freezer. [^1] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/01-cold-storage.md:8
- Leftover cooked meat or poultry: 3 to 4 days in the fridge, 2 to 6 months in the freezer. [^1] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/01-cold-storage.md:9
- Chicken nuggets or patties: 3 to 4 days in the fridge, 1 to 3 months in the freezer. [^1] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/01-cold-storage.md:10
- Pizza: 3 to 4 days in the fridge, 1 to 2 months in the freezer. [^1] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/01-cold-storage.md:11
- Egg, chicken, ham, tuna and macaroni salads: 3 to 4 days in the fridge; they do not freeze well. [^1] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/01-cold-storage.md:12
- Casseroles with eggs, after baking: 3 to 4 days in the fridge, 2 to 3 months in the freezer. [^1] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/01-cold-storage.md:13
- Quiche with filling, after baking: 3 to 5 days in the fridge, 2 to 3 months in the freezer. [^1] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/01-cold-storage.md:14
- Pumpkin or pecan pie, after baking: 3 to 4 days in the fridge, 1 to 2 months in the freezer. [^1] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/01-cold-storage.md:15
- Custard and chiffon pies, after baking: 3 to 4 days in the fridge; do not freeze. [^1] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/01-cold-storage.md:16
- Hard-cooked eggs: 1 week in the fridge; do not freeze. [^1] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/01-cold-storage.md:17
- Raw eggs in the shell: 3 to 5 weeks in the fridge; do not freeze them in the shell (beat yolks and whites together, then freeze). [^1] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/01-cold-storage.md:18
- Raw hamburger and other ground meat or poultry: 1 to 2 days in the fridge, 3 to 4 months in the freezer. [^1] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/01-cold-storage.md:19
- Fresh chicken or turkey pieces: 1 to 2 days in the fridge, 9 months in the freezer. [^1] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/01-cold-storage.md:20
- Fresh beef, veal, lamb and pork steaks, chops and roasts: 3 to 5 days in the fridge, 4 to 12 months in the freezer. [^1] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/01-cold-storage.md:21
- Bacon: 1 week in the fridge, 1 month in the freezer. Raw sausage: 1 to 2 days in the fridge, 1 to 2 months in the freezer. [^1] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/01-cold-storage.md:22
- Luncheon meat, opened or deli sliced: 3 to 5 days in the fridge, 1 to 2 months in the freezer. [^1] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/01-cold-storage.md:23
- Fatty fish such as salmon and tuna: 1 to 3 days in the fridge, 2 to 3 months in the freezer. [^1] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/01-cold-storage.md:24
- Shrimp and crayfish: 3 to 5 days in the fridge, 6 to 18 months in the freezer. [^1] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/01-cold-storage.md:25
- Cooked fish: 3 to 4 days in the fridge, 4 to 6 months in the freezer. [^2] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/01-cold-storage.md:26
- Gravy and meat broth: 1 to 2 days in the fridge, 2 to 3 months in the freezer. [^2] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/01-cold-storage.md:27
- Any other leftovers: 3 to 4 days in the fridge, or 3 to 4 months in the freezer. [^3] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/01-cold-storage.md:28

cards.title: Food and medicine interactions to screen for, and PKU
cards.body:
# Food and medicines, and PKU

## Interactions to screen for (screen and flag; never adjust)
- Warfarin and vitamin K: leafy greens reduce warfarin's effect. The rule is consistency, not avoidance: a steady weekly number of vitamin K servings. [^47] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:245
- Changing vitamin K intake moves INR; cranberry juice raises INR. [^47] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:246
- MAOIs and tyramine: aged cheese and red wine with MAOIs can cause severe high blood pressure and worse. Linezolid and isoniazid act similarly. [^47] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:247
- Grapefruit blocks gut CYP3A4, so more of some drugs enters the blood, and can reduce absorption of others. [^48] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:248
- Affected classes include statins, some calcium-channel blockers, transplant drugs, anti-anxiety drugs, corticosteroids, antiarrhythmics and antihistamines. [^48] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:249
- How strong the effect is varies person to person. [^48] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:250
- Calcium and antibiotics: separate fluoroquinolones by at least 2 hours before or 6 hours after calcium; tetracyclines bind with dairy. [^47] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:252
- Potassium with ACE inhibitors or potassium-sparing diuretics: these already raise potassium, so avoid excess potassium. [^47] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:253
- Any flagged interaction goes to a pharmacist or prescriber. [^48] [^47] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:256

## PKU (phenylketonuria)
- An inherited disorder of phenylalanine hydroxylase, found by newborn screening. [^65] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:231
- A phenylalanine-restricted diet, started within 10-14 days of birth and kept lifelong, is the core of treatment. [^65] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:232
- Target blood phenylalanine is 120-360 µmol/L for life, with dietitian supervision. [^65] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:234
- Total refusal: PKU is metabolic medicine. Explain what it is and route to the metabolic clinic. [^65] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:237
