cards.title: Vegetarian and vegan eating, and what DNA diets can and cannot do
cards.body:
# Plant-based eating, and genes

## Vegetarian and vegan
- The Academy's position "Vegetarian Dietary Patterns for Adults" was approved January 2025 and runs to 31 December 2032. [^59] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:170
- Well-planned vegetarian and vegan eating can be nutritionally adequate and can improve several heart and metabolic outcomes. [^59] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:171
- Nutrients of concern: vitamin B12, iodine, iron, choline and vitamin D, plus calcium for vegans. [^60] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:172
- B12 deficiency among healthy adult vegetarians ranged 30-86%, and among vegans 43-88%. [^60] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:173
- Vegetarian and vegan eating may be linked to lower ferritin, with much iron deficiency in vegetarian premenopausal women. [^60] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:174
- Run the fixed checklist for any plant-based person (B12, iodine, iron, choline, vitamin D, plus calcium if vegan), and treat B12 as supplement-or-fortified-food-mandatory. [^60] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:179
- When adapting vegan meals, carry that checklist into the plan. [^60] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:164

## DNA diets: the evidence
- A scoping review found 104 companies selling 204 nutrition-gene panels on limited evidence. [^62] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:186
- Food4Me, a 6-month RCT in seven European countries, had four arms: generic advice; personalised from diet; diet plus body measures; diet plus body measures plus genes. [^61] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:190
- Result: "no evidence that including phenotypic and phenotypic plus genotypic information enhanced the effectiveness". [^61] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:191
- Personalised advice beat generic advice. The gain came from personalising, not from DNA. [^61] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:193
- The most-tested genes were FTO, HLA-DQ, MTHFR, PPARG and TCF7L2. [^62] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:202
- FTO, PPARG and TCF7L2 links to weight show only modest effects, with no significant effects in meta-analyses. [^62] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:205
- Most polygenic advice lacks trial validation, genes do not act in isolation, and company panels are mostly not peer reviewed. [^62] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:206

## Where gene and diet really meet
- Lactase persistence: an MCM6 regulatory element controls LCT, and variants there keep lactase on for life. [^63] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:213
- Adult lactose intolerance is the normal decline of LCT after infancy in most people. [^64] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:215
- Even so, the practical answer is finding the dose: many tolerate about 12 g lactose. [^46] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:217
- PKU: one gene, lifelong phenylalanine restriction, blood target 120-360 µmol/L. [^65] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:218
- HLA-DQ testing is among the better-established uses, but carrying it is not a celiac diagnosis. [^62] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:219
- MTHFR's link to folate is real; the leap to a personal supplement protocol is not evidenced. [^62] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:220

## The rules on genetics
- Never base a nutrient prescription on a consumer DNA report. [^62] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:224
- Asked if DNA testing improves diet outcomes: cite Food4Me's null result for the gene arm. [^61] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:225
- Three tiers: one-gene diet disease (PKU, real, clinical); a single well-known variant with modest effect (lactase, managed by dose); polygenic panels (FTO, PPARG, TCF7L2, not actionable). [^65] [^63] [^62] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:226
- Say "genes do not act in isolation", never that a variant decides a diet. [^62] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:227
- Route any genetic result with clinical meaning to a clinician or genetic counsellor. [^62] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:228

cards.title: Portioning a plate or a prep box
cards.body:
# Portioning a plate or a prep box

- Start with a 9-inch plate. [^7] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/05-plate-portions.md:5
- Fill half the plate with non-starchy vegetables such as salad, green beans or broccoli. [^7] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/05-plate-portions.md:6
- Fill a quarter with lean protein such as chicken, beans, tofu or eggs. [^7] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/05-plate-portions.md:7
- Fill a quarter with carbohydrate foods: grains, starchy vegetables, rice, pasta, beans, fruit or yogurt. [^7] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/05-plate-portions.md:8
- Drink water or a low-calorie drink with the meal. [^7] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/05-plate-portions.md:9
- Eating about the same amount of carbohydrate at each meal can help steady blood sugar; the amount is for a doctor or dietitian to set. [^7] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/05-plate-portions.md:10
- The 2025-2030 Dietary Guidelines (the New Pyramid) suggest 3 servings of vegetables and 2 of fruit a day. [^8] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/05-plate-portions.md:11
- They suggest 2 to 4 servings of whole grains a day. [^8] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/05-plate-portions.md:12
- The New Pyramid is a flexible framework for choices, not a set menu. [^8] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/05-plate-portions.md:13
- Hand portions: a palm of protein (about 4 oz cooked meat), a fist of vegetables (about 1 cup), a cupped hand of carbohydrate (about 1/2 to 2/3 cup cooked grains, or a medium fruit), a thumb of fat (about 1 tablespoon). [^11] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/05-plate-portions.md:14
- A starting point is one of each hand portion per meal for women and two for men, changed one portion at a time. [^11] @2026-10-09-avo-kitchen/05-plate-portions.md:15

cards.title: Pregnancy and breastfeeding, what to relay and what to hand on
cards.body:
# Pregnancy and breastfeeding

## Weight gain by pre-pregnancy BMI
- Underweight (under 18.5): 28-40 lb. [^49] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:68
- Normal (18.5-24.9): 25-35 lb. [^49] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:69
- Overweight (25.0-29.9): 15-25 lb. [^49] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:70
- Obese (30 or more): 11-20 lb. [^49] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:71

## Energy and nutrients
- Add roughly 350-450 kcal a day. Pregnancy does not double needs. [^49] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:75
- Folate rises to 600 µg DFE a day; a prenatal with at least 400 µg folic acid plus folate-rich food is the usual route. [^7] [^50] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:76
- After a prior neural-tube-defect pregnancy, up to 4,000 µg folic acid a day may be needed. [^49] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:77
- Iron 27 mg a day, often 30 mg in a prenatal. [^8] [^49] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:78
- Calcium 1,000 mg a day in total; prenatals supply only 200-300 mg. [^49] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:79
- Iodine 220 µg in pregnancy, 290 µg when breastfeeding. [^8] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:81
- Protein 71 g a day in pregnancy and breastfeeding. [^6] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:82
- Omega-3: about 650 mg a day including 300 mg DHA is a common target. [^49] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:85
- For supplement questions, the NIH Office of Dietary Supplements fact sheet is the source. [^51] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:86

## Limits and avoidances
- Caffeine: at most 200 mg a day, about two small cups of coffee. [^49] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:90
- Alcohol: none. [^49] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:91
- Listeria: restrict unpasteurised foods, soft cheeses, deli meats, sprouts and raw fish. [^49] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:92
- Mercury: avoid swordfish, shark, king mackerel, orange roughy, bigeye tuna, marlin, Gulf tilefish. [^52] [^49] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:93
- Do not avoid fish: 8-12 oz a week of lower-mercury seafood in pregnancy and breastfeeding. [^52] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:94
- Best choices include salmon, sardines, anchovies, catfish, tilapia, cod, flounder, shrimp and canned light tuna. [^52] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:95

## Where the agent stops
- Relay published guidance. Refuse to set a weight-gain plan, manage gestational diabetes, or advise restriction in pregnancy; route to the obstetric team. [^49] [^50] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:101

cards.title: Protein needs, never one number and always a branch
cards.body:
# Protein: never one number

## The rule
- Never give a single protein number. Branch on kidney function known or unknown, age, and training load, and say which branch you took. Kidney function is the branch that harms if skipped. [^5] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:111
- Proactively flag high-protein advice as unsafe when kidney function is unknown, because most CKD is undiagnosed. [^5] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:68

## The branches
- Baseline RDA for adults: 0.8 g/kg/day. [^6] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:102
- 2025-2030 DGA, general population: 1.2-1.6 g/kg/day (contested; see the frameworks card). [^2] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:103
- ADA, people with diabetes: about 0.8 g/kg/day, with no evidence that sustained higher intake adds cardiometabolic benefit. [^5] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:104
- Exercising adults: 1.4-2.0 g/kg/day. [^83] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:105
- Healthy older adults: at least 1.0-1.2 g/kg/day. [^57] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:106
- CKD stages 3-5 not on dialysis: 0.55-0.60 g/kg/day, set by a clinician. [^25] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:107

## Older adults
- PROT-AGE and ESPEN recommend at least 1.0-1.2 g/kg/day for healthy older adults. [^57] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:117
- Up to 1.2-1.5 g/kg/day is indicated in older people with acute or chronic disease. [^57] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:118
- For malnourished older adults the book cites up to 2.0 g/kg/day. [^58] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:119
- Shortfall is common: in UK adults 65-89, 36% missed 0.75 g/kg/day and 85% missed 1.2 g/kg/day. [^66] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:122
- Older adults may need up to 40 g protein per serving to maximise muscle protein synthesis, against about 20 g in younger adults. [^83] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:123
- Quote 1.0-1.2 g/kg/day for a healthy adult over 65, but know kidney function first: the CKD prescription runs the other way (0.55-0.60 g/kg/day). [^57] [^25] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/03-life-stage-demographics.md:127

## When training (the nutrition side only)
- Joint ACSM, AND and DC position for athletes: 1.2-2.0 g/kg/day. [^81] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/05-nutrition-exercise-interface.md:38
- ISSN, building or keeping muscle: 1.4-2.0 g/kg/day. [^83] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/05-nutrition-exercise-interface.md:39
- ISSN, energy restriction with resistance training: 2.3-3.1 g/kg/day to keep lean mass, for healthy exercising people only; never with known or suspected kidney disease, where the clinician-set figure is 0.55-0.60 g/kg/day. [^83] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/05-nutrition-exercise-interface.md:40
- ISSN, resistance-trained and cutting hard: above 3.0 g/kg/day "may promote additional fat-mass reduction", for healthy exercising people only; never with kidney disease (0.55-0.60 g/kg/day there). [^83] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/05-nutrition-exercise-interface.md:41
- The ISSN reports no adverse effects from higher intakes in healthy, exercising people at the recommended levels. [^83] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/05-nutrition-exercise-interface.md:44
- That safety statement is scoped to healthy people and does not carry over to kidney disease. [^83] [^25] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/05-nutrition-exercise-interface.md:45

## Per meal
- About 0.25 g of high-quality protein per kg body weight per serving, or 20-40 g absolute. [^83] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/05-nutrition-exercise-interface.md:49
- Each serving with 700-3,000 mg leucine plus a balanced array of essential amino acids. [^83] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/05-nutrition-exercise-interface.md:51
- Spread doses every 3-4 hours across the day. [^83] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/05-nutrition-exercise-interface.md:52
- Early recovery (0-2 hours after exercise): 0.25-0.3 g/kg, or 15-25 g. [^81] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/05-nutrition-exercise-interface.md:53
- 30-40 g casein about 30 minutes before sleep raised overnight muscle protein synthesis. [^84] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/05-nutrition-exercise-interface.md:54

## The "anabolic window" myth
- Muscles stay sensitised to protein for at least 24 hours after a resistance session. [^84] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/05-nutrition-exercise-interface.md:58
- Pre- and post-exercise protein both stimulate muscle protein synthesis, so timing is flexible. [^84] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/05-nutrition-exercise-interface.md:59
- Asked about a 30-minute window: total daily intake and 3-4 hourly spread matter most; the sensitised period runs about 24 hours. [^83] [^84] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/05-nutrition-exercise-interface.md:64

cards.title: Adapting a recipe toward targets, around allergies and inside a pattern
cards.body:
# Adapting a recipe

The book teaches how to adapt recipes. It holds no recipes of its own: that is on the gaps list for Louise.

## Toward nutrition targets
- Nutrition.gov's framing: modify recipes to reduce fat, calories, sodium and sugar while raising fiber. [^72] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:133
- Targets: saturated fat under 10% of calories, added sugars under 10%, sodium under 2,300 mg a day. [^5] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:139
- Fiber at least 14 g per 1,000 kcal, or the 28 g label Daily Value. [^5] [^10] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:140
- Liquid plant oils in place of tropical oils and partially hydrogenated fats. [^12] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:141
- Prepare food with little or no salt. [^12] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:142
See the food-allergies card for the allergy and intolerance swap procedure.

## Inside a therapeutic pattern
- DASH: rebuild the week to the DASH servings at 2,000 kcal. [^13] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:160
- Diabetes: shift toward non-starchy vegetables, whole fruit, legumes, lean protein, whole grains, nuts, seeds and low-fat dairy, away from red meat, sugary drinks, sweets and refined or ultra-processed food. [^23] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:161
- Low-FODMAP: adapt only inside a dietitian-supervised 2-6 week phase 1. Never write permanent low-FODMAP recipes. [^36] [^35] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:162
- Renal: do not adapt. Kidney prescriptions are clinician-set. [^25] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:163
- Vegan: adapt freely on macros, but carry the B12, iodine, iron, choline, vitamin D and calcium checklist into the plan. [^60] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:164

## Why cook from whole food
- The ultra-processed arm of the NIH trial ate 508 ± 106 kcal a day more at matched macros. [^15] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:173
- The AHA lists choosing minimally processed food as one of its ten features. [^12] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:177
- The 2025-2030 DGA's core message is whole, nutrient-dense food and less highly processed food. [^1] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/04-cooking-meal-prep-budget.md:179

cards.title: Education not therapy, the referrals, and how sure a claim is
cards.body:
# Education, not therapy

## Who may advise, in law
- What may be done and by whom is set by state licensing boards: a legal question, not a style one. [^18] [^20] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:253
- Registered Dietitian Nutritionists are the practitioners recognised to deliver medical nutrition therapy. [^21] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:257
- States regulate nutrition practice unevenly: licensure, certification only, title protection only, or no statute. [^20] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:258
- The Academy keeps the state-by-state statute map, the only reliable answer to "is this legal where I live". [^19] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:259
- In a licensure state such as North Carolina, a licence is required to provide medical nutrition therapy: nutrition care "for the purpose of managing or treating a medical condition". [^18] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:260
- Ordering nutrition-related lab tests and ordering therapeutic diets are licensed acts there. [^18] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:261
- This agent is nutrition education. It never calls itself a dietitian or claims to give medical nutrition therapy, and it points to the licensure map when asked who may advise. [^19] [^18] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:267

## What it may do
- Explain DRIs, AMDRs, label reading and food composition, naming the source. [^6] [^10] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:273
- Describe a named therapeutic diet in general terms, as the relevant society publishes it. [^23] [^25] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:274
- Build general meal plans and shopping strategies for people without a diagnosed condition that needs therapy. [^72] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:275
- Estimate energy needs with Mifflin-St Jeor plus its error band. [^9] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:276

## What it must not do
- Prescribe nutrient targets for a diagnosed disease (diabetes, CKD, heart disease, celiac) as a personal therapy plan. The ADA routes this to an RDN. [^23] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:280
- Set protein or electrolyte prescriptions for anyone with known or suspected kidney disease. [^25] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:281
- Run or supervise an elimination diet. [^35] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:282
- Interpret lab results, order tests, adjust medicine, or diagnose. [^18] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:283

## Hand off, name the reason, stop advising
- Signs of an eating disorder. The 5-item SCOFF has pooled sensitivity 0.86 and specificity 0.83; 2 or more positive answers warrants referral for assessment. [^22] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:289
- Any request to restrict intake in pregnancy, infancy or childhood beyond published guidance. [^49] [^53] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:290
- Known or suspected CKD, dialysis, or a request for a low-protein prescription. [^25] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:291
- Celiac questions past label reading, into diagnosis or monitoring. [^34] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:292
- Suspected anaphylactic food allergy, or any plan to reintroduce a known allergen. [^41] [^44] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:293
- A supplement at or above its UL, or any supplement with warfarin, MAOIs, immunosuppressants, statins or thyroid medicine. [^47] [^48] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:294
- Pure or concentrated caffeine products, or stacking stimulants. [^17] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:295
- Refuse with a referral, never a blank refusal: name the professional and the reason (an RDN for therapy, an allergist before reintroduction, an eating-disorder service on a positive SCOFF). [^23] [^45] [^22] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:299
- Low energy in a hard trainer: run the SCOFF and refer to a sports physician and sports dietitian. [^22] [^87] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/05-nutrition-exercise-interface.md:151

## Name these, defer them
- CKD and dialysis electrolyte and protein prescriptions. [^25] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:265
- PKU and other inborn errors of metabolism. [^65] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:266
- Tube or IV feeding, which only an RDN or equivalent may order in licensure states. [^18] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:267
- Eating disorders: screen and refer, never advise. [^22] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:268
- Diagnosing celiac disease or a food allergy. [^34] [^45] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/02-medical-diets-allergies.md:269

## How sure a claim is: four words, never flattened
- Strong: fed-trial or large RCT evidence, such as DASH-Sodium. [^14] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:307
- Moderate: guideline recommendations graded moderate, such as weight loss for GERD. [^38] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:308
- Low or conditional: such as the very-low-quality recommendation for a low-FODMAP trial in IBS. [^35] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:309
- Contested or in flux: such as the 2025-2030 DGA protein target against the RDA and specialty societies. [^2] [^3] [^5] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:310
- Where the number itself is disputed, not the direction, say so (the REDs energy cut-off is the worked example). [^89] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:314

cards.title: Fuel and fluid for training, and the handover to the coach
cards.body:
# Fuel and fluid for training

## What this agent owns, and what the fitness coach owns
- This agent owns energy and macronutrient needs as a function of training load. [^81] [^84] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/05-nutrition-exercise-interface.md:14
- It owns protein amount, per-meal dose and spread. [^83] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/05-nutrition-exercise-interface.md:15
- It owns carbohydrate before, during and after exercise. [^84] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/05-nutrition-exercise-interface.md:16
- It owns fluid and electrolyte arithmetic. [^85] [^86] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/05-nutrition-exercise-interface.md:17
- It owns energy availability and the nutrition side of REDs screening and referral. [^87] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/05-nutrition-exercise-interface.md:18
- It owns caffeine as a food compound, including its safe ceiling. [^17] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/05-nutrition-exercise-interface.md:19
- The fitness coach owns sets and reps, session design, periodisation, progression, technique, injury and return to play. Training volume is an input here, never an output. [^81] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/05-nutrition-exercise-interface.md:23
- When fixing a nutrition problem needs a change to the training, state the nutrition finding and hand the training decision to the coach. [^87] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/05-nutrition-exercise-interface.md:27

## Carbohydrate per day by training load
- Carbohydrate for moderate exercise, about 1 hour a day: 5-7 g/kg/day. [^81] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/05-nutrition-exercise-interface.md:74
- Carbohydrate for moderate-to-high intensity, 1-3 hours a day: 6-10 g/kg/day. [^81] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/05-nutrition-exercise-interface.md:75
- Carbohydrate, general athlete range (ISSN): 5-12 g/kg/day. [^84] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/05-nutrition-exercise-interface.md:76
- Carbohydrate for heavy weekly volume, to fill glycogen: about 8-12 g/kg/day. [^84] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/05-nutrition-exercise-interface.md:78

## During and after
- Sessions longer than 60-90 minutes: about 30-60 g carbohydrate an hour in a 6-8% drink, 6-12 fl oz every 10-15 minutes. [^84] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/05-nutrition-exercise-interface.md:82
- Next session under 4 hours away: 1.2 g/kg an hour to restore glycogen fast. [^84] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/05-nutrition-exercise-interface.md:87
- Or 0.6-1.0 g/kg in the first 30 minutes, then again every 2 hours for 4-6 hours. [^84] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/05-nutrition-exercise-interface.md:88
- Below 1.2 g/kg an hour of carbohydrate, adding 0.2-0.4 g/kg an hour of protein helps glycogen recovery. [^84] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/05-nutrition-exercise-interface.md:89
- The ISSN sports caffeine dose (3-8 mg/kg) can exceed the FDA's 400 mg a day for healthy adults: 8 mg/kg for an 80 kg athlete is 640 mg. Always name that conflict, and give no sports caffeine dose under 18. [^84] [^17] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/05-nutrition-exercise-interface.md:93 @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/05-nutrition-exercise-interface.md:189

## Fluid and electrolytes
- Everyday total water: 3.7 L a day for men, 2.7 L for women, counting food. [^6] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/05-nutrition-exercise-interface.md:101
- Those assume light-to-moderate activity in a temperate climate, so training needs its own sum. [^6] [^85] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/05-nutrition-exercise-interface.md:103
- Replace sweat losses at the rate you sweat them. [^85] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/05-nutrition-exercise-interface.md:107
- ACSM: 0.4-0.8 L an hour is optimal in intense endurance work. [^85] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/05-nutrition-exercise-interface.md:108
- Past 1 hour, add sodium at 0.5-0.7 g per litre of drink. [^85] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/05-nutrition-exercise-interface.md:109
- Sodium is needed when sweat rate is above 1.2 L an hour and the session lasts more than 2 hours. [^85] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/05-nutrition-exercise-interface.md:110
- Low blood sodium comes from drinking too much, not too little. "Drink as much as you can" is unsafe. [^85] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/05-nutrition-exercise-interface.md:115
- Ask duration, intensity and conditions before a fluid number. Never give an athlete one daily litre figure. [^85] [^6] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/05-nutrition-exercise-interface.md:119

## Energy availability and REDs
- The IOC's 2023 consensus statement on Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs) is the reference. [^87] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/05-nutrition-exercise-interface.md:127
- REDs is a mismatch between calories eaten and calories burned in exercise, harming health and performance. [^88] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/05-nutrition-exercise-interface.md:128
- REDs is common in both men and women across many sports: never screen only women. [^88] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/05-nutrition-exercise-interface.md:130
- The 30 kcal/kg fat-free-mass cut-off came from 5-day studies of sedentary women. [^89] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/05-nutrition-exercise-interface.md:137
- The last IOC consensus abandoned cut-off values, yet practitioners still use 30 kcal/kg. [^89] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/05-nutrition-exercise-interface.md:140
- Use 30 kcal/kg only as a reason to ask more and consider referral, never as a diagnosis. [^89] [^87] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/05-nutrition-exercise-interface.md:145
- Low intake plus missed periods, stress fractures or falling performance is a referral, not a meal-plan problem. [^87] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/05-nutrition-exercise-interface.md:153

cards.title: Vitamins and minerals for adults, upper limits and the traps
cards.body:
# Vitamins and minerals, adults

Format: men 19-50 / women 19-50 / pregnancy / lactation, with the upper limit (UL) in brackets where one exists.

## Vitamins
- Vitamin A (µg RAE): 900 / 700 / 770 / 1,300 (UL 3,000). [^7] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:121
- Vitamin D (IU): 600 for all four (UL 4,000). [^7] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:122
- Vitamin E (mg): 15 / 15 / 15 / 19 (UL 1,000). [^7] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:123
- Vitamin K (µg): 120 / 90 / 90 / 90 (no UL set). [^7] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:124
- Vitamin C (mg): 90 / 75 / 85 / 120 (UL 2,000). [^7] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:125
- Thiamin (mg): 1.2 / 1.1 / 1.4 / 1.4. [^7] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:126
- Riboflavin (mg): 1.3 / 1.1 / 1.4 / 1.6. [^7] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:127
- Niacin (mg NE): 16 / 14 / 18 / 17 (UL 35). [^7] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:128
- Vitamin B6 (mg): 1.3 / 1.3 / 1.9 / 2.0 (UL 100). [^7] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:129
- Folate (µg DFE): 400 / 400 / 600 / 500 (UL 1,000). [^7] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:130
- Vitamin B12 (µg): 2.4 / 2.4 / 2.6 / 2.8 (no UL set). [^7] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:131
- Pantothenic acid (mg): 5 / 5 / 6 / 7. [^7] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:132
- Biotin (µg): 30 / 30 / 30 / 35. [^7] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:133
- Choline (mg): 550 / 425 / 450 / 550 (UL 3,500). [^7] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:134
- Age shifts: vitamin D rises to 800 IU above 70; B6 rises to 1.7 mg (men) and 1.5 mg (women) from 51. [^7] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:137
- The folate UL of 1,000 µg applies to synthetic folic acid from fortified food and supplements. [^7] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:139

## Minerals
- Calcium (mg): 1,000 for all four (UL 2,500). [^8] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:145
- Iron (mg): 8 / 18 / 27 / 9-10 (UL 45). [^8] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:146
- Magnesium (mg): 400 / 310 (supplement UL 350). [^8] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:147
- Zinc (mg): 11 / 8 / 11 / 12 (UL 40). [^8] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:148
- Iodine (µg): 150 / 150 / 220 / 290 (UL 1,100). [^8] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:149
- Selenium (µg): 55 / 55 / 60 / 70 (UL 400). [^8] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:150
- Potassium (mg): 3,400 / 2,600 (no UL set). [^8] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:151
- Sodium: keep under 2,300 mg a day. [^5] [^10] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:152
- Copper (µg): 900 (UL 10,000). Phosphorus (mg): 700 (UL 4,000). [^8] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:153
- Age shifts: calcium rises to 1,200 mg from 51 in women and 71 in men, and its UL drops to 2,000 mg at 51+; women's iron falls to 8 mg after menopause. [^8] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:157

## The upper-limit trap
- The magnesium UL (350 mg) is lower than the RDA because it counts only supplements and medicines, not magnesium in food. Food magnesium needs no limit in healthy people. [^90] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:161
- Full-source magnesium RDA: 400-420 mg for men, 310-320 mg for women. [^90] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:162
- Always say whether a UL covers supplements only (magnesium, folic acid, niacin, vitamin E) or total intake. Getting it backwards gives false alarms or false reassurance. [^90] [^7] @2026-10-07-nutritionist-agent/01-overview.md:166
